As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives. Methodology BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3). Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage. Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards. Learning from demonstrations (SFT) We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called. Learning from teachers (MOPD) Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4). Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three. Learning from rules and environments (RL stages) Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth. The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling. Data composition Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use. Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability. Results Tool use & agents BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5). Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× BFCL v4¹ 44.0 23.4 37.7 28.1 22.8 ACEBench² 58.7 30.1 55.4 39.4 24.5 τ-bench³ 51.5 23.2 46.5 6.5 28.8 Claw-Eval⁴ 46.5 39.3 48.9 31.6 31.0 BrowseComp-Plus⁵ 4.5 1.9 2.8 0.2 0.8 ToolSandbox⁶ 64.6 30.5 41.2 45.7 28.1 Average 45.0 24.7 38.8 25.3 22.7 Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined ; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Knowledge Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× GPQA Diamond⁷ 38.1 33.2 59.9 35.0 15.8 MMLU-Pro⁸ 48.9 41.6 65.5 39.4 40.0 Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Instruction following BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× IFEval⁹ 90.8 59.7 80.0 85.6 78.4 IFBench⁹ 55.9 22.0 40.9 33.9 40.6 Multi-IF¹⁰ 67.2 43.2 66.9 68.2 53.4 Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Multi-turn conversations The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1). Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5. Weak spots BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8). Where it works: app-level performance breakdown BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ. Single tool calls work well everywhere Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70). Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups. The largest gains are in multi-step tasks On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks. Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14). Inference efficiency BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer. Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each. Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9): τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer). It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks. Intended Use and Limitations BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty . BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics. items.content: Back to Articles Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models Published November 11, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 37 +31 Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors! Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget. In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4 , my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how. This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study , which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example. Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below. Table of Contents Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors Token Pooling Choosing a Pooling Budget Calibrating Adaptive Pooling Token Pooling-Aware Training A Loss Wrapper in Sentence Transformers Optional Kernel Acceleration Using the Trained Model Evaluation Results Combining Compression Techniques References Code and Models Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document. For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together: MaxSim ⁡ ( Q , D ) = ∑ q ∈ Q max ⁡ d ∈ D q ⊤ d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim ( Q , D ) = q ∈ Q ∑ ​ d ∈ D max ​ q ⊤ d Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID , storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision. The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together. Token Pooling HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering . Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors. These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring. You can make compression proportional to document length: from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor= 4 ) With pool_factor=4 , documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged. Choosing a Pooling Budget HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls: Setting What it expresses max_tokens=16 A maximum of 16 vectors per document, including protected tokens. pool_factor=4 Approximately one quarter of each document's original vectors. distance_threshold=... A shared Ward merge-distance threshold, allowing vector counts to vary with embedding geometry. This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4 , a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold , the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved. Calibrating Adaptive Pooling Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective . Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents : from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling model = MultiVectorEncoder( "lightonai/LateOn" ) calibration_embeddings = model.encode_document(calibration_documents) threshold = HierarchicalTokenPooling.calibrate_distance_threshold(calibration_embeddings, target_tokens= 16 ) pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(distance_threshold=threshold) # Apply pooling, targeting an average of 16 vectors per document document_embeddings = model.encode_document(documents_to_index, token_pooling=pooling) Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus. Token Pooling-Aware Training Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that. If you've used Matryoshka embeddings , the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors. For my example, each training batch contributes two losses: Retrieval using the original document embeddings. Retrieval after compressing documents to approximately one quarter of their original vectors. Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below. items.content: Back to Articles The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 46 +40 Suvaditya Mukherjee suvadityamuk Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository . If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. How TRELLIS.2 works Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. Planning Which components to fine-tune We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities. Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training. If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Why use LoRA Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub: Give the containers access to your data. Set the parameters for your task. Run the preprocessing container. Run the fine-tuning container. Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training. Experiment overview We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment: Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images. Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration. Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models. We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it. Walkthrough Running on Hugging Face Jobs Preprocessing The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline . See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository . export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep \ --meshes your-username/my-meshes \ --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --private --holdout 0.05 \ --views 16 --workers 8 For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments: flag meaning -d Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id> --flavor a100-large The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware --timeout 6h The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to --secrets HF_TOKEN Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image cr.hf.co/...:latest The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here . The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later. LoRA Fine-tuning The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run. We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 If you set --push-to , the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity . A compact script is also available in the same repository . If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have , feel free to use the following set of commands. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For the Shape Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Running locally with Docker Preprocessing The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different. # For preprocessing into latents docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep --meshes your-username/my-meshes --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 LoRA Fine-tuning # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands: export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso Inside the training pipeline Preprocessing into latents We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning. cfg = json.load( open ( { "ss" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json" , "shape" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json" , }[FLOW] ) ) key, latents = { "ss" : ( "ss_latent" , "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64" ), "shape" : ( "shape_latent" , "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512" ), }[FLOW] roots = json.dumps( { "gso" : { key: f" {DATA} / {latents} " , "render_cond" : f" {DATA} /renders_cond" , "meta" : DATA, } } ) ds = getattr (datasets, cfg[ "dataset" ])(roots, **cfg[ "dataset_args" ]) holdout = set ( open ( f" {DATA} /holdout.txt" ).read().split()) ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout] batches = cycle( DataLoader( ds, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle= True , drop_last= True , num_workers= 4 , collate_fn= getattr (ds, "collate_fn" , None ), ) ) Preparing LoRA adapters We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate job

The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. Planning Which components to fine-tune We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities. Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training. If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Why use LoRA Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub: Give the containers access to your data. Set the parameters for your task. Run the preprocessing container. Run the fine-tuning container. Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training. Experiment overview We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment: Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images. Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration. Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models. We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it. Walkthrough Running on Hugging Face Jobs Preprocessing The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline . See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository . export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep \ --meshes your-username/my-meshes \ --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --private --holdout 0.05 \ --views 16 --workers 8 For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments: flag meaning -d Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id> --flavor a100-large The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware --timeout 6h The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to --secrets HF_TOKEN Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image cr.hf.co/...:latest The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here . The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later. LoRA Fine-tuning The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run. We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape \ --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 If you set --push-to , the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity . A compact script is also available in the same repository . If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have , feel free to use the following set of commands. export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name ss_lora \ --push-path ss_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For the Shape Flow DiT hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large -- timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --run-name shape_lora \ --push-path shape_lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Running locally with Docker Preprocessing The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different. # For preprocessing into latents docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \ trellis2-prep --meshes your-username/my-meshes --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 LoRA Fine-tuning # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config ss --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands: export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso Inside the training pipeline Preprocessing into latents We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning. cfg = json.load( open ( { "ss" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json" , "shape" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json" , }[FLOW] ) ) key, latents = { "ss" : ( "ss_latent" , "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64" ), "shape" : ( "shape_latent" , "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512" ), }[FLOW] roots = json.dumps( { "gso" : { key: f" {DATA} / {latents} " , "render_cond" : f" {DATA} /renders_cond" , "meta" : DATA, } } ) ds = getattr (datasets, cfg[ "dataset" ])(roots, **cfg[ "dataset_args" ]) holdout = set ( open ( f" {DATA} /holdout.txt" ).read().split()) ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout] batches = cycle( DataLoader( ds, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle= True , drop_last= True , num_workers= 4 , collate_fn= getattr (ds, "collate_fn" , None ), ) ) Preparing LoRA adapters We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate job

items.content: Back to Articles Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run Published November 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 109 +103 Célina Hanouti celinah Follow Victor Mustar victor Follow Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. What's next This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face. More tasks routed through OpenRouter. Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started. Can we use Hugging face any model online and use in our programs? Thanks. See translation Reply Pauliehedron 1 day ago • edited 1 day ago Does your version follow the cache-hit price or does it force us to keep constantly watching and blocking providers who game the input and output pricing to harvest the cache-hit and the full cache-miss? Because openrouter themselves you have to have a full non fine grained admin key and monitor yourself or else put in guardrails and lock to providers or put in your own local proxies to do the monitoring with the admin key. Which is quite a burden for a service taking a 5:5% cut like openrouter does. Are you doing the same???
