Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. What's next This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face. More tasks routed through OpenRouter. Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started. items.content: Back to Articles DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency Team Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 19 +13 Jason Chen jzsc Follow RadixArk Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0 : BF16 FP8 NVFP4 The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. Run DaisyRose-27B We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "http://localhost:30000/v1" , api_key= "none" , ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model= "DaisyRose-27B" , messages=[ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "How many positive divisors does 360 have?" , } ], temperature= 1.0 , top_p= 0.95 , extra_body={ "top_k" : 20 , "min_p" : 0.0 }, ) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.reasoning_content) print (response.choices[ 0 ].message.content) The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . Benchmark results Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B Terminal Bench 4.1 5.6 12.0 Terminal Bench 2.1 73.0 75.5 DeepSWE v1.1 42.2 46.2 SWE Bench Pro v2 91.3 94.7 HLE (text-only) 33.9 34.3 IFBench 79.5 82.4 GPQA Diamond 89.2 90.7 DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. High-quality training data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. We selected tasks using three criteria: Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran Qwen3.8-27B on every task and redesigned each one around the mistakes we wanted the model to stop making. We then adjusted the difficulty until the solve rate fell within a useful learning range. Each task requires several interdependent steps. The agent has to reason, plan, and execute across a long job. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox, with more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens. Tasks must reward actually solving the problem. We reviewed every task alongside the model’s attempts. Tasks that could be passed without solving the intended problem, or that contained a design flaw, were fixed or removed. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization. 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs. Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady. Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs. Robust sandbox service Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently . The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%. Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine. Try the model or train your own Download DaisyRose-27B , follow the SGLang serving guide , or use Miles to train your own agents. We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab. We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor. Adapted from the original RadixArk article . items.content: Back to Articles Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases Enterprise Article Published November 18, 2026 Upvote 26 +20 Nicholas Fuller nfuller Follow ibm-research Sean Falconer thefalc Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Bilge Zeren Aksu bzeren Follow ibm-research Julian Payne Pyjamacardinal Follow ibm-research Mountu Jinwala mjinwala Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Chandra Reddy creddyhf Follow ibm-research Vijay Ekambaram vijaye12 Follow ibm-research Arindam Jati ajati Follow ibm-research Robert Metzger rmetzger0 Follow ibm-research Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.( documentation ). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs. The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made. See how time series and real-time context come together to create value: Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening. A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere. Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate. Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them. This approach can help teams in four ways: - Scale model development . A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one. - Refresh predictions as data changes . Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration. - Put signals closer to decisions . Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment. - Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment. Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent Mission-critical use cases across real-enterprises The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic. Use Case 1 | Production optimization: every tub in spec An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result. To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range. When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails. The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills. Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment. Use Case 2 | Anomaly detection: from a flag to the right action A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus. AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store. When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes. Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged. Use Case 3 | Supply chain planning: every SKU, every store, every hour A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock. With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point. When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand. Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk. Use Case 4 | Fraud and security: every card has its own normal Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends. A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules. The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review. Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow. Use Case 5 | Trading: pace the order with the tape An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average. On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk. If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail. Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order. Use Case 6 | Semantic search: find every signal that looks like this A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant. TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions. This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself. Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals. Industry Specific Applications The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries: Industrial AI: from sensor to setpoint. The plant manager wants every batch in spec and no line stopped by a surprise. SCADA, QA lab and energy meter streams are forecast as they arrive. Production optimization moves the setpoints when quality starts to drift, anomaly detection flags the reading no rule was written for, and semantic search finds every pump that showed the same pattern before a failure. Setpoints, work orders and alerts reach the floor inside the cycle, not at the next shift report. Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data. Retail: a store and its supply chain. The store manager wants a full shelf on Saturday without overstock on Monday. Sales, weather and promotion streams are forecast for every product in every store. Supply chain planning sets the order, anomaly detection catches the empty shelf or the missed delivery, and fraud and security holds the suspicious card. Orders, store tasks and holds go out before the shelf runs empty. Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data. Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume. Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be. In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Chandra Reddy creddyhf Follow ibm-research Vijay Ekambaram vijaye12 Follow ibm-research Arindam Jati ajati Follow ibm-research Robert Metzger rmetzger0 Follow ibm-research Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.( documentation ). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs. The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made. See how time series and real-time context come together to create value: Streamhouse: real-time data and intelligence for agentic era Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening. A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state. Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere. Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate. Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them. This approach can help teams in four ways: - Scale model development . A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one. - Refresh predictions as data changes . Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration. - Put signals closer to decisions . Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment. - Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment. Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent Mission-critical use cases across real-enterprises The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic. Use Case 1 | Production optimization: every tub in spec An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result. To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range. When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails. The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills. Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment. Use Case 2 | Anomaly detection: from a flag to the right action A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus. AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store. When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes. Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged. Use Case 3 | Supply chain planning: every SKU, every store, every hour A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock. With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point. When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand. Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk. Use Case 4 | Fraud and security: every card has its own normal Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends. A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules. The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review. Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow. Use Case 5 | Trading: pace the order with the tape An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average. On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk. If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail. Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order. Use Case 6 | Semantic search: find every signal that looks like this A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant. TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions. This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself. Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals. The plant manager wants every batch in spec and no line stopped by a surprise. SCADA, QA lab and energy meter streams are forecast as they arrive. Orders, store tasks and holds go out before the shelf runs empty. Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. items.content: Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 15 +9 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 . To try it, install Transformers from that PR: pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head" Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: path = snapshot_download( "tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming" ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( f" {path} /dense" , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map={ "" : "mps" , "experts.*" : "disk" }, quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits= 8 ), experts_offload={ "cache_bytes" : 12 << 30 , "quantized_experts" : f" {path} /experts-q3" , }, ) That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script : the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table. Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So: experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16) the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping. The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming , on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s. Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 10.0 tok/s 14.8 1.5x Prefill, 4K prompt 68 tok/s 220 3.2x Decode after a 6K document 7.3 tok/s 13.7 1.9x Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page . I also tried vllm-metal , vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache. Closing the gap Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped: Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch. Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet and the hyper-connections. Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights , reducing dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size. Prefill , we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed. Long documents : attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token. Misses : Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer, while the SSD would otherwise be idle. Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now: These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 13.9 tok/s 14.8 1.06x Prefill, 4K prompt 228 tok/s 220 1.0x Decode after a 6K document 12.4 tok/s 13.7 1.1x That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers. Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it. Conclusion It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work. Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader , and prebuilt kernels from the Hub . All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub , and the project loads them from there. Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time. The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717 , and the benchmarks are in the Space . Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome. Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM. Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata . Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went. items.raw_text: Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 15 +9 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 . To try it, install Transformers from that PR: pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head" Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: path = snapshot_download( "tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming" ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( f" {path} /dense" , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map={ "" : "mps" , "experts.*" : "disk" }, quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits= 8 ), experts_offload={ "cache_bytes" : 12 << 30 , "quantized_experts" : f" {path} /experts-q3" , }, ) That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script : the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table. Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So: experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16) the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping. The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming , on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s. Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 10.0 tok/s 14.8 1.5x Prefill, 4K prompt 68 tok/s 220 3.2x Decode after a 6K document 7.3 tok/s 13.7 1.9x Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page . I also tried vllm-metal , vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache. Closing the gap Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped: Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch. Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet and the hyper-connections. Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights , reducing dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size. Prefill , we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed. Long documents : attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token. Misses : Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer, while the SSD would otherwise be idle. Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now: These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 13.9 tok/s 14.8 1.06x Prefill, 4K prompt 228 tok/s 220 1.0x Decode after a 6K document 12.4 tok/s 13.7 1.1x That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers. Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it. Conclusion It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work. Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader , and prebuilt kernels from the Hub . All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub , and the project loads them from there. Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time. The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717 , and the benchmarks are in the Space . Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome. Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM. Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata . Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went. items.summary: Back to Articles Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 Reson8 reson8-thomas Follow Reson8 Mark 't Hart MarktHart Follow Reson8 Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModel
items.content: Back to Articles Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 Reson8 reson8-thomas Follow Reson8 Mark 't Hart MarktHart Follow Reson8 Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Runs anywhere : native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM, no custom code 40+ languages : automatic language detection Output control : numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, forced language Extremely fast : an hour of audio in about half a second, with over 7,000 RTFx on full batches Holds up on real phone calls : on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark Quickstart Transcribe with 🤗 Transformers uv pip install torch transformers accelerate from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request( audio= "https://hf.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/bcn_weather.mp3" , language= "English" , # omit to detect automatically ).to(model.device, dtype=model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 512 ) generated = output[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ]:] print (processor.decode(generated, return_format= "transcription_only" )[ 0 ]) # return_format="parsed" if detecting language audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these. How it's built Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On-policy distillation with GOLD Results Accuracy for its size On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . The best score for its size Speed Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Real phone calls Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER , on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better. Real phone calls, 14 English accents Try it The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash . It's also available through our API . We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.26607 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation Authors: Deepali Singh , Deepesh Parpani , Aviral Gupta View a PDF of the paper titled Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation, by Deepali Singh and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM \cite{b1}, can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM's frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder's representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation.
