items.content: Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation Deepali Singh, Deepesh Parpani, Aviral Gupta Affiliation: College of Information and Computer Sciences University of Massachusetts Amherst Amherst, USA {deepalisingh, dparpani, aviralgupta}@umass.edu Abstract Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM [ 1 ] , can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM’s frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder’s representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation. Source Code is available here: Google Drive Link Index Terms: Human activity recognition, inertial measurement units, synthetic data augmentation, diffusion models, self-supervised learning, token embeddings, cross-subject generalization, wearable sensing I Introduction Human activity recognition (HAR) from wrist-worn inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors supports a range of health monitoring and behavioral analysis applications. Despite strong benchmark performance, cross-subject generalization remains a persistent challenge as classifiers trained on one subject population frequently fail on unseen individuals, a gap directly measured by leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation. Synthetic data augmentation offers one path toward broader generalization, yet generating realistic IMU signals directly is difficult given complex temporal structure, subject-specific motion styles, and device-placement variability. An alternative is to generate in a pretrained model’s representation space, where activity-relevant structure is already encoded. Bio-PM [ 1 ] , a Transformer encoder pretrained via masked movement-segment reconstruction on the NHANES wrist-IMU corpus (approximately 28,000 hours, 11,000 participants), provides this foundation. Its token space is semantically organized by activity and exhibits no subject-level clustering, making it a natural target for class-conditional generation without subject conditioning. We train class-conditional generative decoders directly in Bio-PM’s token space, using the frozen encoder as a quality oracle. A key challenge is that Bio-PM produces contextual, BERT-like representations in which each of the 192 tokens per window encodes global temporal context, making this a richer but more complex distribution to model than a standard latent space. We develop and compare two decoders: (1) CAR-IMU, a Class-conditional AutoRegressive decoder, and (2) CD-IMU, a Class-conditional Diffusion decoder, evaluating both distributional realism and downstream LOSO classification utility on the WISDM benchmark. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • We propose CAR-IMU, which generates synthetic Bio-PM token sequences autoregressively, and characterize a distributional shift requiring per-class affine calibration to resolve. • We design CD-IMU, a diffusion decoder that eliminates the calibration dependency of CAR-IMU, achieving high distributional realism without post-hoc correction. • We provide systematic generation quality analysis across both decoders using cosine similarity, Fréchet distance (FD) in Bio-PM token space, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), variance ratio, and Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) evaluation. • We demonstrate that augmenting a LOSO HAR classifier with CD-IMU synthetic tokens, using a 320-dimensional feature representation and confusion-aware augmentation, yields statistically significant improvements over the real-only baseline across 51 subjects on WISDM. • We present a PatchDecoder for approximate reconstruction of raw IMU waveforms from synthetic token sequences, extending the pipeline toward signal-level synthesis. II Dataset and Bio-PM II-A WISDM Dataset We use the WISDM wrist accelerometer dataset [ 2 ] , comprising recordings from 51 subjects performing six activities: Walking, Jogging, Upstairs, Downstairs, Sitting, and Standing. Raw signals are sampled at 20 Hz and segmented into non-overlapping 10-second windows, yielding 12,514 windows with approximately balanced class distribution. All experiments follow a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, training on 50 subjects and evaluating on the held-out subject across all 51 folds. II-B Bio-PM Encoder Pipeline Each window is encoded using two frozen Bio-PM modules. The accelerometer encoder applies a bandpass filter and projects the signal into 192 movement-element patches, each represented as a 64-dimensional token embedding via a bidirectional Transformer, producing a token sequence of shape 192 × 64 192\times 64 . The gravity encoder applies a low-pass filter and maps the DC component to a 64-dimensional gravity embedding via a CNN, and appends it as a key to the same token_store.h5. Neither encoder is fine-tuned at any stage so they serve exclusively as a frozen feature extractor and quality oracle for generation. II-C Bio-PM Token Space Inspection Fig. 1 : UMAP activity clusters on real data tokens generated by Bio-PM To validate the token space before training any decoder, we compute nearest-neighbor same-class accuracy and visualize the mean-pooled token embeddings using UMAP. As shown in Fig. 1 , activity classes form well-separated clusters with no subject-level structure. A nearest-neighbor classifier achieves 90% same-class accuracy in this space, confirming semantic richness. The absence of subject separation means that a decoder conditioned only on activity class is sufficient, and no subject conditioning is required. These properties make Bio-PM’s token space a viable target for class-conditional generation. Despite approximate class balance ( ≈ \approx 16.6% per class), the dataset exhibits significant representation overlap. Baseline analyses reveal high confusion rates between activities sharing fundamental motion patterns: Walking and Upstairs are confused 22%–27% of the time, while Downstairs is confused with Sitting and Standing up to 23% of the time. III CAR-IMU: Autoregressive Decoder III-A Architecture and Training CAR-IMU is a class-conditional autoregressive transformer that generates synthetic Bio-PM token sequences one position at a time. A learned activity-specific prefix token CLS_c is prepended to the token sequence, providing class conditioning. The model consists of four causal Transformer layers with multi-head attention, where each position attends only to preceding positions. An output projection head maps each hidden state back to the 64-dimensional token space. Training follows a next-token prediction objective using mean squared error (MSE) loss, with teacher forcing applied during training and autoregressive rollout at inference. The model is trained for 50 epochs using AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule on the 12,514 real token sequences from the token store. The resulting model has 137K trainable parameters, with all Bio-PM encoder weights frozen throughout. III-B The Calibration Problem Raw CAR-IMU tokens exhibit a distributional shift from real tokens. While centroid directions are roughly aligned, per-class means and variances differ measurably. We quantify generation realism using Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) evaluation, where an MLP classifier is trained entirely on synthetic tokens and tested on real data. Uncalibrated CAR-IMU tokens yield a TSTR macro-F1 of 0.22, confirming the shift is large enough to mislead a downstream classifier. To close this gap, we apply per-class affine calibration, shifting and scaling each synthetic class distribution to match the mean and standard deviation of the corresponding real class: x ^ = x − μ syn , c σ syn , c ⋅ σ real , c + μ real , c \hat{x}=\frac{x-\mu_{\text{syn},c}}{\sigma_{\text{syn},c}}\cdot\sigma_{\text{real},c}+\mu_{\text{real},c} (1) After calibration, TSTR macro-F1 improves to 0.63 (more details in Table V ), demonstrating that the representational structure is present but distributionally offset. While calibration resolves the shift post-hoc, it requires access to real token statistics and does not address the underlying generation gap. III-C Architectural Limitations While computationally efficient and highly effective for high-variance locomotion activities, the CAR-IMU architecture introduces structural challenges beyond distributional shift: • Class Signal Fading: Because the class embedding is only injected at position 0, the conditioning signal dilutes over the 192-step sequence. • Autoregressive Drift: Prediction errors compound over time. This disproportionately affects static and less periodic activities (e.g., Sitting, Standing, Downstairs) that lack the self-correcting periodic rhythms naturally found in activities like Walking. Together, these limitations, (1) distributional shift requiring post-hoc calibration, (2) class signal fading, and (3) autoregressive error compounding, motivate CD-IMU: a diffusion-based decoder that conditions on class identity at every denoising step and learns the full token distribution directly, without relying on calibration. IV CD-IMU: Class-Conditional Diffusion Decoder IV-A Architecture CD-IMU is a class-conditional denoising diffusion model operating over Bio-PM token sequences. The forward process adds Gaussian noise to real token sequences over T = 1000 T=1000 timesteps using a linear schedule ( β 1 = 10 − 4 \beta_{1}=10^{-4} , β T = 0.02 \beta_{T}=0.02 ). The reverse process is parameterized by an 8-layer bidirectional Transformer that directly predicts the clean token sequence x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} from the noisy input x t x_{t} , the timestep t t , and the activity class c c . Class and timestep conditioning are applied at every layer via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) [ 3 ] , modulating each layer’s activations using scale and shift parameters from a concatenated class and sinusoidal timestep embedding. This ensures class conditioning persists throughout the full network depth, directly addressing the signal fading of CAR-IMU. Bidirectional attention with no causal mask is consistent with Bio-PM’s contextual encoding. The training objective combines three losses: ℒ = ℒ x 0 + w ⁡ ( e ) ​ ( ℒ dist + ℒ freq ) \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{x_{0}}+w(e)\left(\mathcal{L}_{\text{dist}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{freq}}\right) (2) where ℒ x 0 \mathcal{L}_{x_{0}} is the MSE between predicted and real clean tokens, ℒ dist \mathcal{L}_{\text{dist}} is a per-class mean and variance alignment term, ℒ freq \mathcal{L}_{\text{freq}} penalizes spectral discrepancy along the sequence axis, and w ⁡ ( e ) w(e) is a linear warmup weight ramped from 0 to 1 over the first 15 epochs to prevent regularization from dominating before the model learns basic denoising. Generation uses deterministic DDIM sampling [ 4 ] with 200 steps. IV-B Architectural Ablation An earlier variant introduced a Spectral FFN branch and an aggressive spectral loss coefficient β freq = 5.0 \beta_{\mathrm{freq}}{=}5.0 , causing the spectral loss to dominate reconstruction at a ratio of approximately : 1 1369\!:\!1 and preventing convergence. Additionally, checkpointing on validation loss caused the best checkpoint to be saved at epoch 1 due to a favorable initialization, yielding a model that generated class-agnostic tokens. CD-IMU resolves these failures by reducing β freq \beta_{\mathrm{freq}} to 0.05 0.05 , removing the Spectral FFN, applying uniform regularization weights across classes, and checkpointing on average cosine similarity from periodic generation evaluations rather than validation loss. V Classification Experiments V-A CAR-IMU Augmentation Strategies We evaluate CAR-IMU synthetic tokens across four augmentation experiments that vary calibration, feature dimensionality, and augmentation strategy. Features are extracted from the 192-token sequence in four configurations as summarised in Table I . Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM [ 1 ] , can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM’s frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder’s representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation. Source Code is available here: Google Drive Link Index Terms: Human activity recognition, inertial measurement units, synthetic data augmentation, diffusion models, self-supervised learning, token embeddings, cross-subject generalization, wearable sensing I Introduction Human activity recognition (HAR) from wrist-worn inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors supports a range of health monitoring and behavioral analysis applications. Despite strong benchmark performance, cross-subject generalization remains a persistent challenge as classifiers trained on one subject population frequently fail on unseen individuals, a gap directly measured by leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation. Synthetic data augmentation offers one path toward broader generalization, yet generating realistic IMU signals directly is difficult given complex temporal structure, subject-specific motion styles, and device-placement variability. An alternative is to generate in a pretrained model’s representation space, where activity-relevant structure is already encoded. Bio-PM [ 1 ] , a Transformer encoder pretrained via masked movement-segment reconstruction on the NHANES wrist-IMU corpus (approximately 28,000 hours, 11,000 participants), provides this foundation. Its token space is semantically organized by activity and exhibits no subject-level clustering, making it a natural target for class-conditional generation without subject conditioning. We train class-conditional generative decoders directly in Bio-PM’s token space, using the frozen encoder as a quality oracle. A key challenge is that Bio-PM produces contextual, BERT-like representations in which each of the 192 tokens per window encodes global temporal context, making this a richer but more complex distribution to model than a standard latent space. We develop and compare two decoders: (1) CAR-IMU, a Class-conditional AutoRegressive decoder, and (2) CD-IMU, a Class-conditional Diffusion decoder, evaluating both distributional realism and downstream LOSO classification utility on the WISDM benchmark. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • We propose CAR-IMU, which generates synthetic Bio-PM token sequences autoregressively, and characterize a distributional shift requiring per-class affine calibration to resolve. • We design CD-IMU, a diffusion decoder that eliminates the calibration dependency of CAR-IMU, achieving high distributional realism without post-hoc correction. • We provide systematic generation quality analysis across both decoders using cosine similarity, Fréchet distance (FD) in Bio-PM token space, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), variance ratio, and Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) evaluation. • We demonstrate that augmenting a LOSO HAR classifier with CD-IMU synthetic tokens, using a 320-dimensional feature representation and confusion-aware augmentation, yields statistically significant improvements over the real-only baseline across 51 subjects on WISDM. • We present a PatchDecoder for approximate reconstruction of raw IMU waveforms from synthetic token sequences, extending the pipeline toward signal-level synthesis. II Dataset and Bio-PM II-A WISDM Dataset We use the WISDM wrist accelerometer dataset [ 2 ] , comprising recordings from 51 subjects performing six activities: Walking, Jogging, Upstairs, Downstairs, Sitting, and Standing. Raw signals are sampled at 20 Hz and segmented into non-overlapping 10-second windows, yielding 12,514 windows with approximately balanced class distribution. All experiments follow a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, training on 50 subjects and evaluating on the held-out subject across all 51 folds. II-B Bio-PM Encoder Pipeline Each window is encoded using two frozen Bio-PM modules. The accelerometer encoder applies a bandpass filter and projects the signal into 192 movement-element patches, each represented as a 64-dimensional token embedding via a bidirectional Transformer, producing a token sequence of shape 192 × 64 192\times 64 . The gravity encoder applies a low-pass filter and maps the DC component to a 64-dimensional gravity embedding via a CNN, and appends it as a key to the same token_store.h5. Neither encoder is fine-tuned at any stage so they serve exclusively as a frozen feature extractor and quality oracle for generation. The absence of subject separation means that a decoder conditioned only on activity class is sufficient, and no subject conditioning is required. These properties make Bio-PM’s token space a viable target for class-conditional generation. Despite approximate class balance ( ≈ \approx 16.6% per class), the dataset exhibits significant representation overlap. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.26598 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher Authors: Yang Meng , Zixin Ding , Robert L. Grossman , Yuxin Chen View a PDF of the paper titled Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher, by Yang Meng and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment. Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher Yang Meng Zixin Ding Robert L. Grossman Yuxin Chen Abstract Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor’s error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90 % 90\% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment. The privileged oracle runs only at training time; the student is the only component that deploys. Modality pool (top): the acquisition policy chooses among distinct diagnostic tests with heterogeneous per-test costs. Training time (left): the privileged oracle is a myopic, deterministic Brier algorithm with access to the label y i y_{i} and the unobserved candidate value x ( a ) x^{(a)} ; for each sampled ( x i , S ) (x_{i},S) it ranks the candidates, and the deployable student policy π ϕ ​ ( a ∣ 𝐱 S , 𝐦 S ) \pi_{\phi}(a\mid\mathbf{x}_{S},\mathbf{m}_{S}) is trained to reproduce that ranking by soft-KL distillation under a random-mask prior. Deployment (right): the student selects the next modality under the remaining budget, with no oracle recomputation and no access to y y or x ( a ) x^{(a)} . The pretrained predictor f θ f_{	heta} produces the final diagnosis. In many applications, obtaining the feature values of a data instance is not free. A clinical diagnosis draws on tests that differ widely in monetary cost, turnaround time, and invasiveness ( Ma et al. 2019 ) ; discovering a new material or molecule requires costly wet-lab experiments or simulations, each consuming reagents, compute, or instrument time ( Shahriari et al. 2016 ; Meng et al. 2026a ; Ding et al. 2024 ; Ding et al. 2026 ) ; and a sensing or robotic platform must spend power, time, or motion for each measurement ( Krause et al. 2008 ) . Therefore, acquiring the full feature set for every instance is often infeasible, and even when it is possible the cost rarely justifies the marginal gain. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) ( Ma et al. 2019 ) addresses this by learning to select, for each instance, a small and informative subset of features to acquire, maximizing predictive performance under a fixed acquisition budget. Progress in the field has come from increasingly sophisticated ways of constructing an acquisition objective : an information reward under a partial generative model ( Ma et al. 2019 ) , conditional mutual information estimated by a learned network ( Covert et al. 2023 ; Gadgil et al. 2024 ) , a non-parametric acquisition oracle ( Valancius et al. 2024 ) , or long-horizon return optimized by reinforcement learning ( Shim et al. 2018 ; Zannone et al. 2019 ) . Despite the algorithmic diversity, all of these methods share a structural property: the supervision signal is self-constructed – these methods both define the acquisition objective and optimize toward it, and the acquisition policy is never supervised by an external teacher. This naturally raises a question. At training time we already have access to information the deployed policy never sees: the true label, and the actual values of the candidates that have not been acquired, which are exactly the ingredients a myopic acquisition oracle needs to rank candidates in closed form. If that supervision is available for free, why spend the algorithmic effort designing yet another surrogate? We instead construct the acquisition teacher explicitly , as a deterministic algorithm that scores each candidate by the error the downstream predictor would incur were it acquired. We then train a deployable student to reproduce the teacher’s ranking. Distilling a teacher’s ranking into a student is a known method, but prior work splits into two families that our setting sits between. On the one hand, in capacity distillation the teacher is a learned, larger model and the students exist to cut inference cost as in ranking distillation for recommendation ( Tang and Wang 2018 ; Reddi et al. 2021 ) and reranker compression for large language models ( Sun et al. 2023 ) . On the other hand, in privileged-information distillation the teacher can see inputs the students cannot access at test time and the student aims to close that information gap rather than to save compute ( Lopez-Paz et al. 2015 ) . OracleImitator belongs to the second family and sharpens it in two aspects to tailor for AFA settings. First, our teacher is not a learned model but a closed form oracle computed from the training labels and the unacquired feature values, so there is no teacher to train and thus no teacher approximation error. Second, the distillation object is a budget-constrained acquisition ranking, so the student is re-queried at each partial-observation state and only its top candidate is acquired per step. The resulting student, OracleImitator , is a mask-conditioned network trained by soft-KL under a random-mask prior, and it never sees the label or the unacquired feature values at test time (Figure 1 ). Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmarks ( Schütz et al. 2025 ) , six datasets in total, this approach matches or outperforms specialized utility-learning methods across the budget range, and on the medical cohort recovers 90 % 90\% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Making the teacher an explicit algorithmic object also makes it analyzable. Once the teacher is a concrete mapping from observed state to ranked action, we can ask questions the AFA literature could not previously address directly: how much of the teacher’s behavior is recoverable by a student that sees only what is visible at deployment, how student quality depends on the teacher it distils, and which alternative explanations for the residual oracle gap can be excluded by controlled ablations. Contributions. 1. We reframe AFA as learning from an explicit privileged acquisition teacher rather than from a self-constructed utility surrogate (Section 2 , formalized in Section 4 ). 2. We introduce OracleImitator , a deployable student policy trained by soft-target distillation from a myopic Brier oracle under a random-mask prior (Section 4 ), and show it matches or outperforms specialised utility learners across six datasets (Section 5 ). 3. We use the explicit teacher as an instrument to study the AFA problem itself, reporting a teacher-quality sweep (Section 5.4 ), an empirical teacher-learnability diagnostic, and controlled ablations that exclude architecture, predictor, cost scheme, and generalization as explanations for the observed saturation (Section 6 ). 2 Related Work Active feature acquisition (AFA). AFA methods generate their acquisition supervision internally and differ mainly in how. One line of work optimizes a self-constructed utility (as stated in Section 1 ): EDDI ( Ma et al. 2019 ) uses an information-theoretic acquisition reward under a partial VAE, Covert et al. (2023) amortize the greedy conditonal-mutual-information policy, and DIME ( Gadgil et al. 2024 ) estimates the conditional mutual information itself. AACO ( Valancius et al. 2024 ) applies a nonparametric acquisition-conditioned oracle at inference, whereas we distill an offline privileged oracle into a separate deployable policy. A second line of work formulates acquisition as sequential decision-making problem and optimizes a policy by RL ( Shim et al. 2018 ; Zannone et al. 2019 ; Kachuee et al. 2019 ; Jain et al. 2025 ) . These methods differ in what they optimize, utility versus return, but not in where the signal comes from: the target is designed, not distilled from a teacher. A recent benchmark further finds that the RL-based methods often train unstably and do not consistently outperform simpler greedy or oracle-based alternatives ( Schütz et al. 2025 ) . Learning from teachers. A separate line of work learns from an existing supervisor. Imitation learning and behavior cloning ( Pomerleau 1988 ; Ross et al. 2011 ; Osa et al. 2018 ) distil an expert’s demonstrations; learning using privileged information ( Vapnik and Izmailov 2015 ; Vapnik and Vashist 2009 ) transfers a training-time-only signal to the deployed model; and knowledge distillation ( Hinton et al. 2015 ; Bucilă et al. 2006 ) matches a student to a pretrained teacher model. In all cases, these works study how to transfer knowledge from an existing teacher, rather than whether such a teacher can be constructed in the first place. Prediction under missing modalities. Predicting from an arbitrary observed subset is complementary to AFA: mask-aware predictors trained under random feature masking produce a label from whatever has been acquired ( Schütz et al. 2025 ; Gadgil et al. 2024 ; Covert et al. 2023 ) . We take such a predictor as given and study only which modalities to acquire for it. 3 Problem Setup 3.1 Setting Let x = ( x ( 1 ) , … , x ( K ) ) ∈ ℝ d x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(K)})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be a feature vector partitioned into K K modalities , the units at which acquisition happens. In our motivating medical cohort a modality is a distinct diagnostic test (a clinical, transcriptomic, or histology panel), each separately orderable; in the tabular benchmarks a modality is an individual feature. A designated set FREE ⊆ [ K ] \mathrm{FREE}\subseteq[K] is available at no cost as c k = 0 c_{k}=0 for k ∈ FREE k\in\mathrm{FREE} . In the medical setting these are the demographics recorded at intake. This objective rejects direct optimization in two ways. First, it is non-differentiable, as π \pi enters only through the discrete set S π S_{\pi} and accuracy is an indicator. Second, it is not a property of π \pi alone: whether a subset was worth acquiring depends on f θ f_{	heta} , and how far down the acquisition order the policy is evaluated depends on B B . We instead exploit the fact that a good acquisition order is easy to identify with training-time information: given y y and the full 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , one can compute directly how much each candidate modality would change the downstream error under f θ f_{	heta} . What is hard is identifying it deployably , from 𝐱 S \mathbf{x}_{S} alone. We therefore compute the signal offline on the training data and learn a deployable policy that imitates it, as described in the next section. 4 Method: OracleImitator The objective in Equation 1 is hard to optimize but easy to evaluate offline: given a label and a full feature vector, the effect of each candidate modality on the downstream error can be measured directly, even though neither the label nor the unacquired values is available at deployment. Our method. We treat the offline computation as a teacher and learn a deployable student that imitates it. On training data, we score every unacquired modality by the error the shared predictor would incur if that modality were added, and turn the scores into a ranking over candidates. We then train a policy that sees only the observed subset and its mask to reproduce that ranking. The teacher is discarded after training and the student is deployable as-is. 4.1 The teacher For a training pair ( x i , y i ) (x_{i},y_{i}) and observed subset S S , the teacher scores each candidate a ∉ S a

Following the terminology of Vapnik and Izmailov (2015) , the teacher is privileged in two ways, both of which disqualify at deployment: it reads the label y i y_{i} , and it reads the value x ( a ) x^{(a)} of a modality it has not paid for. Why a myopic teacher? A natural alternative is a finite-horizon oracle that plans several acquisitions ahead. We use the one step version instead, for two reasons. First, it is well-defined given nothing but the trained f θ f_{	heta} , whereas a planning oracle introduces its own search hyperparameters and its own approximation error. Second, on our datasets the gains from non-myopic planning are limited, consistent with the benchmark finding that this benefit is strongly dataset-dependent ( Schütz et al. 2025 ) . We revisit this choice in Appendix A.1 . Why this makes distillation easy. Two properties of teacher matter for downstream accuracy. First, it is an algorithm rather than a fitted model: given ( x i , y i , S ) (x_{i},y_{i},S) and f θ f_{	heta} , its scores are determined. There is no teacher to train on and no teacher approximation error between the student and the objective, in contrast to distilling a trained network ( Hinton et al. 2015 ; Vapnik and Izmailov 2015 ) . Second, the f θ f_{	heta} inside the teacher is the same predictor the student passes through at deployment, so the acquisition signal is measured on the model that will actually be scored. No auxiliary per-mask classifier is trained. 4.2 The student The student π ϕ ​ ( a ∣ 𝐱 S , 𝐦 S ) \pi_{\phi}(a\mid\mathbf{x}_{S},\mathbf{m}_{S}) conditions only on the observed subset and its mask, which makes it deployable by construction. It is a small mask-conditioned MLP mapping [ 𝐦 S ⊙ 𝐱 , 𝐦 S ] [\mathbf{m}_{S}\odot\mathbf{x},\mathbf{m}_{S}] through a shared trunk into an action head , with one logit per candidate, and an auxiliary classifier head used only during training as a multi-task regularizer ( Caruana 1997 ; Kendall et al. 2018 ; Ding et al. 2024 ) . At deployment we take argmax \operatorname*{argmax} over the unobserved, affordable candidates from the action head and discard the outputs of classifier head. Training the action head is behavior cloning of the teacher ( Pomerleau 1988 ) : we minimize cross-entropy against the teacher’s selection on states drawn from randomly masked subsets. Because random masking exposes the student to a broad range of reachable partial-observation states, it mitigates the covariate shift that motivates interactive imitation learning ( Ross et al. 2011 ) . Appendix A details the widths, depths and parameter counts of the MLP. 4.3 Training and deployment Which subsets should the student see? Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher Yang Meng Zixin Ding Robert L. Grossman Yuxin Chen Abstract Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor’s error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90 % 90\% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment. The pretrained predictor f θ f_{	heta} produces the final diagnosis. In many applications, obtaining the feature values of a data instance is not free. A clinical diagnosis draws on tests that differ widely in monetary cost, turnaround time, and invasiveness ( Ma et al. 2019 ) ; discovering a new material or molecule requires costly wet-lab experiments or simulations, each consuming reagents, compute, or instrument time ( Shahriari et al. 2016 ; Meng et al. 2026a ; Ding et al. 2024 ; Ding et al. 2026 ) ; and a sensing or robotic platform must spend power, time, or motion for each measurement ( Krause et al. 2008 ) . Therefore, acquiring the full feature set for every instance is often infeasible, and even when it is possible the cost rarely justifies the marginal gain. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) ( Ma et al. 2019 ) addresses this by learning to select, for each instance, a small and informative subset of features to acquire, maximizing predictive performance under a fixed acquisition budget. Progress in the field has come from increasingly sophisticated ways of constructing an acquisition objective : an information reward under a partial generative model ( Ma et al. 2019 ) , conditional mutual information estimated by a learned network ( Covert et al. 2023 ; Gadgil et al. 2024 ) , a non-parametric acquisition oracle ( Valancius et al. 2024 ) , or long-horizon return optimized by reinforcement learning ( Shim et al. 2018 ; Zannone et al. 2019 ) . Despite the algorithmic diversity, all of these methods share a structural property: the supervision signal is self-constructed – these methods both define the acquisition objective and optimize toward it, and the acquisition policy is never supervised by an external teacher. This naturally raises a question. At training time we already have access to information the deployed policy never sees: the true label, and the actual values of the candidates that have not been acquired, which are exactly the ingredients a myopic acquisition oracle needs to rank candidates in closed form. If that supervision is available for free, why spend the algorithmic effort designing yet another surrogate? We instead construct the acquisition teacher explicitly , as a deterministic algorithm that scores each candidate by the error the downstream predictor would incur were it acquired. We then train a deployable student to reproduce the teacher’s ranking. Distilling a teacher’s ranking into a student is a known method, but prior work splits into two families that our setting sits between. On the one hand, in capacity distillation the teacher is a learned, larger model and the students exist to cut inference cost as in ranking distillation for recommendation ( Tang and Wang 2018 ; Reddi et al. 2021 ) and reranker compression for large language models ( Sun et al. 2023 ) . On the other hand, in privileged-information distillation the teacher can see inputs the students cannot access at test time and the student aims to close that information gap rather than to save compute ( Lopez-Paz et al. 2015 ) . OracleImitator belongs to the second family and sharpens it in two aspects to tailor for AFA settings. First, our teacher is not a learned model but a closed form oracle computed from the training labels and the unacquired feature values, so there is no teacher to train and thus no teacher approximation error. Second, the distillation object is a budget-constrained acquisition ranking, so the student is re-queried at each partial-observation state and only its top candidate is acquired per step. The resulting student, OracleImitator , is a mask-conditioned network trained by soft-KL under a random-mask prior, and it never sees the label or the unacquired feature values at test time (Figure 1 ). Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmarks ( Schütz et al. 2025 ) , six datasets in total, this approach matches or outperforms specialized utility-learning methods across the budget range, and on the medical cohort recovers 90 % 90\% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Making the teacher an explicit algorithmic object also makes it analyzable. Once the teacher is a concrete mapping from observed state to ranked action, we can ask questions the AFA literature could not previously address directly: how much of the teacher’s behavior is recoverable by a student that sees only what is visible at deployment, how student quality depends on the teacher it distils, and which alternative explanations for the residual oracle gap can be excluded by controlled ablations. Contributions. 1. We reframe AFA as learning from an explicit privileged acquisition teacher rather than from a self-constructed utility surrogate (Section 2 , formalized in Section 4 ). 2. We introduce OracleImitator , a deployable student policy trained by soft-target distillation from a myopic Brier oracle under a random-mask prior (Section 4 ), and show it matches or outperforms specialised utility learners across six datasets (Section 5 ). 3. We use the explicit teacher as an instrument to study the AFA problem itself, reporting a teacher-quality sweep (Section 5.4 ), an empirical teacher-learnability diagnostic, and controlled ablations that exclude architecture, predictor, cost scheme, and generalization as explanations for the observed saturation (Section 6 ). 2 Related Work Active feature acquisition (AFA). AFA methods generate their acquisition supervision internally and differ mainly in how. One line of work optimizes a self-constructed utility (as stated in Section 1 ): EDDI ( Ma et al. 2019 ) uses an information-theoretic acquisition reward under a partial VAE, Covert et al. (2023) amortize the greedy conditonal-mutual-information policy, and DIME ( Gadgil et al. 2024 ) estimates the conditional mutual information itself. AACO ( Valancius et al. 2024 ) applies a nonparametric acquisition-conditioned oracle at inference, whereas we distill an offline privileged oracle into a separate deployable policy. A second line of work formulates acquisition as sequential decision-making problem and optimizes a policy by RL ( Shim et al. 2018 ; Zannone et al. 2019 ; Kachuee et al. 2019 ; Jain et al. 2025 ) . These methods differ in what they optimize, utility versus return, but not in where the signal comes from: the target is designed, not distilled from a teacher. A recent benchmark further finds that the RL-based methods often train unstably and do not consistently outperform simpler greedy or oracle-based alternatives ( Schütz et al. 2025 ) . Imitation learning and behavior cloning ( Pomerleau 1988 ; Ross et al. 2011 ; Osa et al. 2018 ) distil an expert’s demonstrations; learning using privileged information ( Vapnik and Izmailov 2015 ; Vapnik and Vashist 2009 ) transfers a training-time-only signal to the deployed model; and knowledge distillation ( Hinton et al. 2015 ; Bucilă et al. 2006 ) matches a student to a pretrained teacher model. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.26521 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting Authors: Tara Sowrirajan , Yanqiao Wang View a PDF of the paper titled The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting, by Tara Sowrirajan and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe's gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned -0.0004. For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window. items.content: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting Tara Sowrirajan † † thanks: Corresponding author: tarastar@amazon.com Yanqiao Wang Affiliation: Amazon Abstract In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw + 0.070 +0.070 – 0.107 0.107 log-space R 2 R^{2} in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10 % 10\% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe’s gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72 % 72\% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted + 0.014 +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned − 0.0004 -0.0004 . For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window. 1 Introduction The usual levers for a sequence model are more data, more parameters and a newer architecture ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , while history length is usually fixed or treated as a capacity setting (§ 3 ). We compare them on an industrial task, forecasting a customer’s activity from their event history ( Fader et al., 2005 ; Wang et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2022 ) , and of the levers we tested, history length, the one usually fixed, moves accuracy most. Two lessons carry over. A longer window changes who is scored, biasing raw comparisons either way; scoring every window on one matched cohort removes that bias on the test side (training cohorts still grow). A cheap ridge fit on activity aggregates shows the history gain on every dataset we tried (toy model in § C ). Whether any of these levers binds is not a new question. How much event history a churn model needs has been asked directly ( Ballings and Van den Poel, 2012 ) , and observation-window sufficiency is under active study (§ 3 ). However, the question is rarely answered under controlled conditions. Interventions ship sequentially, on moving populations, and improvements can be hard to attribute when several parts of the modeling pipeline change at once. We run a controlled comparison of these commonly modified axes. We hold fixed the export, the test anchor weeks, the target (364-day forward activity, log ⁡ ( 1 + y ) \log(1{+}y) -transformed, scored in log-space R 2 R^{2} ), and the evaluation. We then sweep, one factor at a time, the axes the field usually credits: model family (eight, from a single-feature linear model to a decay-gated recurrent model ( Mei and Eisner, 2017 ) ), population scale (the nominal 1M/5M/10M sampling tiers, § 4.1 ), capacity, and training objective. The training recipe is held fixed within each family but not across families (Table 13 ). We also sweep the length of the observation window, and it is the largest lever we measured. We internally registered four falsifiable commitments on whether the window gain survives matching and how it bends as the window grows, each with its falsifier fixed before the evaluation that decided it. The one fully blind prediction failed on its own falsifier, and the other three held (Table 1 ). Doubling the observation window from 8 to 16 weeks moves log-space R 2 R^{2} by + 0.070 +0.070 – 0.107 0.107 at the 1M tier in every family we train. The families are the transformer, GRU ( Cho et al., 2014 ) , LSTM ( Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ) , time-biased attention, a decay-gated recurrent model ( Mei and Eisner, 2017 ) , boosted trees ( Ke et al., 2017 ) , a 6-feature ridge, and a single-feature linear model. Time-biased attention replaces the ODE-evolved keys and values of ContiFormer ( Chen et al., 2023b ) with a learned time-decay bias on the attention logits. The two continuous-time baselines, labeled ContiFormer and Neural Hawkes in our tables, are simplified stand-ins for the cited models. In the main runs the inter-event interval they consume is identically zero, so their time mechanisms contributed nothing (§ E.5 ). On this end-anchored export, where every input window ends at the week its forecast is made from, doubling the window also shifts which calendar months the input covers (§ 6 ). The other levers move the metric substantially less (Figure 1 ). Among them, the training objective and time representation (the transformer’s positional encoding) give the largest gains. Both are smaller than the window gain, and we quantify them below. Moving from the nominal 1M to the 10M sampling tier changes sequence-model levels by ≤ 0.006 \leq 0.006 , seed 42. The exception is the 6-feature ridge, whose level dips 0.016 0.016 – 0.028 0.028 at 10M while its window gain stays intact (§ 2.7 ). The recurrent models train on a fixed-size sample at every tier, so their differences across tiers measure population composition at a fixed training-set size rather than a response to more data (§ 2.1 ). The measured window gain is similar across the population tiers we evaluate: + 0.0737 +0.0737 at 10M vs. + 0.0731 +0.0731 at 1M (both 3-seed, Huber). Doubling width or depth moves the metric by ≤ 0.005 \leq 0.005 at 8 weeks, seed 42. Against the window’s + 0.070 +0.070 – 0.107 0.107 gain, the observed customer-scale and capacity changes are approximately an order of magnitude smaller. These are one-factor-at-a-time bounds inside the fixed 2-layer, width-128 (d128) recipe, except that the realized learning-rate schedule is not matched across tiers (§ 6 ). We scale customers at fixed capacity and capacity at fixed data (1M tier), and never grow capacity and data together, so we measure no compute-optimal configuration. Two of our own measurements are also about as large as these bounds. The three-seed detection floor for this class, 0.0059 0.0059 , sits above the architecture band reported below and within a factor of 1.2 1.2 of the customer-scale and capacity bounds. Re-selecting checkpoints in log space, the space we report in, moves validation scores by + 0.002 +0.002 to + 0.009 +0.009 . The top of that range exceeds every one of these bounds, and the shift does not cancel out of the capacity contrast. These three axes are therefore bounded but unresolved, and we read none of them as a null (§ 6 ). In these experiments, observation-window length moved the metric by roughly an order of magnitude more than sequence-architecture choice did, on observed effect sizes rather than interval bounds. With the Huber objective at M16 (a 16-week window), five sequence architectures land within ∼ 0.005 {\sim}0.005 of each other with their clocks as built ( 0.5525 0.5525 / 0.5522 0.5522 / 0.5508 0.5508 / 0.5478 0.5478 / 0.5474 0.5474 , seed 42, full test split). A separate test that gives each continuous-time model a working clock detects no gain for ContiFormer and helps Neural Hawkes, by + 0.0116 +0.0116 (95% t t interval over three seeds + 0.0102 +0.0102 to + 0.0130 +0.0130 ), about twice that band. These paired runs are not bridged to the main ones, so where Neural Hawkes would land among the five with a working clock is not measured (§ E.5 ). Because those baselines ran at their own training budgets, we read that band within families rather than as a cross-family ranking (§ 2.7 ). With the MSE objective and 3-seed means, the three families we retrained land within ∼ 0.0025 {\sim}0.0025 (transformer 0.5875 0.5875 / GRU 0.5863 0.5863 / LSTM 0.5850 0.5850 , § 2.8 ). The architecture spread observed at shorter windows narrows substantially by 16 weeks: the decay-gated recurrent model starts 0.015 0.015 below the transformer at 8 weeks and closes most of that gap by 16 weeks (seed 42). Through 16 weeks, matching the test customers across windows makes the window gain larger (§ 2.3 ). We re-evaluate the already-trained checkpoints on matched cohorts , which hold the same customer-weeks at every window, with identical targets and a constant R 2 R^{2} denominator. The matched Δ \Delta (M16 − - M8) is + 0.096 +0.096 , against + 0.075 +0.075 on the full set (Huber, seed 42 for both; the 3-seed full delta is + 0.073 +0.073 ). The raw 8-to-16-week comparison understates the gain in every objective and family measured, and the same pattern holds at 10M ( + 0.094 +0.094 matched vs. + 0.075 +0.075 full); both matched ladders replicate at three seeds. A confound we do not resolve. A longer window changes more than composition. The calendar months the input covers move with it. Every test forecast is made from one of three anchor weeks, four weeks apart ( 2025-02-24 , 2025-03-24 , 2025-04-21 ; § 4.1 ). Each input window ends at one of these three dates, all inside a single ≈ 8 {\approx}8 -week band, so lengthening the window can only extend it backward into particular calendar months. Only at the earliest anchor does an 8-week window cross the turn of the year, and then by two days. At that anchor, 16 weeks is the shortest window we test that reaches the prior November, which the latest anchor reaches only at 24 weeks. The 24- and 32-week windows reach into the preceding autumn and summer. Window length and calendar coverage are therefore not separated in this design, against a target that is a 364-day forward aggregate. The matched cohorts, the activity decomposition, and the objective and family sweeps all hold those three anchor weeks fixed, and the Taobao dataset (§ 2.12 ) spans nine days in total. We therefore ran an anchor-varying control. That control is void under its own registered criterion. When we vary which calendar months the added block covers, the 8-to-16-week gain is + 0.18731 +0.18731 at the 2025-02-24 anchor, + 0.14910 +0.14910 at 2025-03-24 and + 0.04793 +0.04793 at 2025-04-21 for MSE seed 123, and + 0.21159 / + 0.16369 / + 0.05818 +0.21159/{+}0.16369/{+}0.05818 for MSE seed 456. At both seeds the gain is monotone in calendar position, the ordering a seasonal mechanism predicts. The earliest-minus-latest contrast is + 0.13938 +0.13938 (customer-clustered bootstrap 95% CI [ + 0.12459 , + 0.15432 ] [+0.12459,+0.15432] ) and + 0.15341 +0.15341 (95% CI [ + 0.13851 , + 0.16930 ] [+0.13851,+0.16930] ), both excluding zero, and a 200-draw same-cohort placebo that shuffles the anchor labels never attains it. We nonetheless do not interpret it, because the criterion we committed before running the control fails in every setting. That criterion voids the contrast if the per-anchor R 2 R^{2} spread at M8, before the added block enters, exceeds 0.010 0.010 . At both objectives and three seeds each ( 6 6 settings, 18 18 per-anchor values) the spread is 0.0562 / 0.0562 / 0.0623 0.0562/0.0562/0.0623 on MSE and 0.0367 / 0.0378 / 0.0420 0.0367/0.0378/0.0420 on Huber. That is 3.7 3.7 – 6.2 × 6.2\times the bound, so the criterion voids all six. The numbers show why the criterion exists. In all six settings the anchors are ordered identically by baseline difficulty and by calendar position (M8 R 2 = 0.224 / 0.248 / 0.280 R^{2}=0.224/0.248/0.280 at MSE seed 123). The anchor with the most headroom is therefore also the one whose added block covers the holiday period, and we cannot exclude headroom as an explanation of the ordering. Algebraically, 37 37 – 46 % 46\% of each contrast is carried by the M8 model, which contains no added block at all. On Huber, the latest anchor’s added eight weeks are worth − 0.00451 -0.00451 to + 0.01407 +0.01407 , small or slightly negative. We report every per-anchor figure in this paragraph only as a record of what failed and by how much. We do not interpret any of them as a calendar measurement. These figures come from the uniquely keyed matched cohort, the n = 233,038 n=233{,}038 rows with a unique target value in each window’s test split. Its selection drops the zero-target rows, so its levels are not comparable to any full-set R 2 R^{2} . In a post-hoc check we renormalize each anchor’s gain by its own remaining variance, ( R 2 ​ ( 16 ) − R 2 ​ ( 8 ) ) / ( 1 − R 2 ​ ( 8 ) ) (R^{2}(16)-R^{2}(8))/(1-R^{2}(8)) . The two MSE seeds’ earliest/latest ratios then move only from 3.91 3.91 to 3.63 3.63 and from 3.64 3.64 to 3.36 3.36 , so a proportional headroom effect accounts for roughly 7 7 – 8 % 8\% of the ordering. That check does not change the void verdict. The window gain’s direction holds in every pooled analysis we report and at every anchor on MSE. Its magnitude, however, remains confounded with calendar coverage and is not identified as a calendar-independent history effect (§ 6 ). We conclude from the control that, on this end-anchored export, the test anchors in one eight-week band cannot separate window length from calendar coverage at either objective. For the transformer runs, a calendar-balanced test set cannot be recovered from this export. For the weekly-aggregate ridge probe of § E.4 , and only for it, the export’s training period partly separates window length from calendar coverage. We refit the probe on training-period anchors and score it on held-out training customers. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10 % 10\% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe’s gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72 % 72\% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted + 0.014 +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned − 0.0004 -0.0004 . For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.26514 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi Authors: Aishwarya Gunjal , Kanchan Khemnar , Pawan Poojary , Pranav Kulkarni , Raviraj Joshi , Manish Khodaskar View a PDF of the paper titled Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi, by Aishwarya Gunjal and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. We present a bilingual search system for Maharashtra government schemes and public services that combines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. Evaluation on manually curated bilingual queries compares BM25, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using IndicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879 with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding dense-only systems achieve 0.663 and 0.655. MahaSBERT-based fusion also increases precision from 0.781 to 0.808 while matching BM25 recall at 0.946. These results support the complementary use of lexical and semantic signals in this collection, while showing that improvements over a strong lexical baseline are modest and metric-dependent. The study provides an application-focused analysis of hybrid retrieval for bilingual public-service information access. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.26624 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience Authors: Weihao Cheng View a PDF of the paper titled PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience, by Weihao Cheng View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting. items.content: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience Weihao Cheng Email: weihao.cheng@proton.me Abstract Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting. Website: https://xt4d.github.io/playcraft-web Code: https://github.com/xt4d/PlayCraft 1 Introduction Recent AI agents can generate playable games from human instructions ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , but making these games engaging remains difficult. A central source of engagement is mastery, which is the process of developing strategies and skills to overcome the challenges of a game ( Koster, 2004 ) . A game supports mastery when players initially achieve limited success but reach substantially better results as they become more proficient. This progression motivates repeated play, but designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We therefore study how to automatically generate games that support mastery. Prior work generates games that reward stronger play by using play results from computational players to guide designs ( Togelius and Schmidhuber, 2008 ; Nasir et al., 2026 ) . However, the strategies these players find through search or game-specific training may differ from those people develop, making their behavior less representative of human play. Other systems use feedback from repeated playtests to revise generated games ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . These systems prioritize overall game quality, with limited explicit focus on player learning through practice. Recent agents based on foundation models, such as GPT-6 Astra ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , can play 2D and 3D games directly from rendered frames ( Yu, 2026 ; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2026 ) . They perceive only what the game shows, act through the same controls as human players, and can learn from earlier experience. They can also report their understanding of the game and the difficulties they encounter. These capabilities make them suitable simulated players whose experience can shape challenges that reward skillful play. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that starts from an initial playable game and alternates between playing and crafting stages. In the playing stage, a foundation-model player agent observes rendered frames and interacts with the game through the provided controls. It plays a series of episodes, gaining experience with the mechanics and challenges it encounters. The game resets between attempts, while the player agent retains its memory and the lessons it has learned. After each episode, it writes a report covering its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to diagnose and revise the game to promote engagement through mastery. It first estimates the baseline abilities that the player agent has before playing the game. Using these abilities and the observed play, it estimates player performance in the current game at beginner, intermediate, and expert levels. It then identifies gaps between these estimates and a target progression, defined by performance anchors relative to the expected expert outcome. Lastly, it addresses these gaps by revising the game to provide meaningful opportunities for better decisions and execution, while preserving the objectives and core identity of the game. We conduct experiments covering ten 2D and 3D games with varied execution and planning demands. The games are evaluated at three agent intelligence settings using the visual play protocol from the playing stage. We use gains in agent performance across episodes as a proxy for mastery, assuming that the learning patterns of the player agent resemble those of human players. Each episode ends when the game reaches a defined endpoint or the active play budget T T is exhausted. These results must come from strategies that would remain advantageous without the time limit. The second is to give players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. The game should make the benefits, costs, and risks of different choices clear and allow expected performance to continue rising as players gain skill. Active play budget. We assume that players have a finite active play budget T T , which can be set arbitrarily large. Introducing T T provides a reference range for player performance, allowing the crafter agent to identify and address gaps between estimated performance and the anchors. Changing T T can affect the progression of the resulting game because the crafter uses play observed within that budget as evidence for its design. Diagnosis. The crafter agent reads the game instruction, the play records of all available runs, and the archived history of earlier iterations. Because E E episodes may not suffice for the player agent to reach expert-level performance, the crafter agent cannot determine the 100% reference directly from the records. Changing T T can affect the progression of the resulting game because the crafter uses play observed within that budget as evidence for its design. Diagnosis. The crafter agent reads the game instruction, the play records of all available runs, and the archived history of earlier iterations. Because E E episodes may not suffice for the player agent to reach expert-level performance, the crafter agent cannot determine the 100% reference directly from the records. It therefore first estimates the baseline abilities that the player agent has before playing the game, including screen perception, control execution, and strategy discovery. A player without prior experience of a game is not necessarily unskilled. From these abilities and the observed play, it estimates the expected results of beginner, intermediate, and expert players in the current game and compares them with the anchors. Where the estimates deviate from the anchors, it diagnoses the causes, considering entry difficulty; demands on understanding, perception, and execution; opportunities for strategic choice; reward structure; challenge progression; and performance ceiling. If an earlier proposal exists, it also checks which expectations in that proposal the new records support, contradict, or leave untested. It then chooses between building on the earlier direction and exploring a new one. Proposal. The crafter agent then writes a focused design proposal. It prioritizes distinctive changes or additions that enable new strategies and meaningful choices while preserving the defining interactions of the game. It keeps the design coherent and simple, weighing the learning benefit of each rule against the complexity it adds. It builds challenges on the baseline abilities of the player rather than assuming that unfamiliar mechanics alone will limit beginner performance. The revised game must remain visually clear, conveying objects, actions, and consequences through presentation and behavior rather than added indicators. The proposal describes each change and the findings that motivate it. It also states the expected experience and results for beginner, intermediate, and expert players, along with the basis and uncertainty of those estimates. Implementation. In a separate session, the crafter agent implements the proposal. For each proposed change, the crafter identifies the intended player-facing outcome and specifies observable acceptance checks. It then modifies the game code, implementing foundational changes before those that depend on them. It verifies the result by running builds and automated checks, exercising the affected gameplay, and inspecting the affected visuals in the actual renderer. It then corrects any discrepancies. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.26590 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models Authors: Jiahao Huang , Jun Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models, by Jiahao Huang and Jun Wang View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements. We do not claim that these models possess consciousness or subjective experience.
