We do not claim that these models possess consciousness or subjective experience. Jiahao Huang Jun Wang Jiahao Huang 1 Jun Wang 2† 1 Imperial College London, UK 2 University College London, UK † Corresponding author. Abstract Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information to perform a range of multimodal tasks, but their outputs do not reveal the models’ internal concept representations. In brain science, global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from multiple parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to different specialised processes. In this work, we investigate multimodal concept processing in VLMs in relation to these global workspace functions. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens that combines vision encoder and language decoder lenses. Both lenses map intermediate states into a shared semantic space defined by the decoder’s output vocabulary, allowing us to compare concept accessibility across visual and language processing. MC-Lens also supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. Our experiments address four related aspects. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and can be selectively accessed according to task demands. We extend the “readout carriers” from a single name token to a set of tokens, to better capture and express concept information and support subsequent counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that the concept information we access is not only readable, but also participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space based metrics to track cross-modal concept alignment. In controlled VLM training, these metrics reflect its development more clearly than hidden state cosine. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later in training than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects, despite differences in internal organisation. Together, these findings provide an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial systems, and open a way to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal alignment. Figure 1 : Our proposed Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens). The vision encoder lens (V-Lens) reads object and colour concepts across image patches, while the language decoder lens (L-Lens) tracks how the question changes concept accessibility in the decoder. Both use a shared output vocabulary. Decoder numbers are vocabulary ranks, with smaller values indicating greater concept accessibility. 1 Introduction Vision-language models (VLMs) can effectively integrate visual and textual information to perform a range of multimodal tasks ( Alayrac et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . For example, we can ask a VLM to identify an object in an image or describe its colour, and these questions require the model to extract different information from the same image and integrate it with the textual query. However, although current VLMs can readily answer these questions, their outputs do not reveal their internal concept representations. A VLM can also answer a visual question incorrectly even when the visual information needed to answer it remains readable from its intermediate states ( Fu et al., 2025 ) . Existing interpretability methods aim to identify information in internal states and examine its role in producing model outputs ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; Neo et al., 2025 ; Kaduri et al., 2025 ) . Gurnee et al. (2026) proposed the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens), a Jacobian-based method that provides vocabulary-based readouts of intermediate language-model states. Specifically, it maps the model’s intermediate hidden states into the space of final-layer decoder states via averaged Jacobian matrices, and provides concept directions for counterfactual intervention experiments. Using J-Lens, Gurnee et al. (2026) identify functional and structural properties associated with a global workspace in large language models (LLMs). In brain science, global workspace theory (GWT) ( Baars, 2005 ; Baars and Franklin, 2007 ; Dehaene et al., 1998 ) is an influential theory of consciousness that explains how information from different sources is integrated to support flexible cognition. The core hypothesis of this theory is that information is selected from the multiple parallel processes in the brain, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to different specialised processes. Building on the J-Lens study, we extend this analysis to concept information expressed through different modalities, and processed across the visual and language components of VLMs. In this paper, we introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens that combines a vision encoder lens (V-Lens) and a language decoder lens (L-Lens). V-Lens can access concept information from intermediate vision encoder states before visual information is combined with the text input in the decoder. L-Lens can access concept information from decoder states during the integration of visual and textual inputs, allowing us to examine selective access under different text queries and during autoregressive generation. Both V-Lens and L-Lens map intermediate states into a shared semantic space defined by the decoder’s output vocabulary, so we can compare concept accessibility during multimodal information integration and processing. Figure 1 illustrates these readouts in a visual question answering (VQA) example. We conduct counterfactual experiments using MC-Lens, where we intervene on intermediate state components associated with the accessed concepts and observe the resulting model outputs, to infer the role of these concepts in downstream computation. In addition, we also investigate the functional properties and internal organisation of multimodal concept processing in VLMs in relation to GWT. Specifically, our experiments address four related aspects. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Our experiments show that multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and can be selectively accessed according to task demands. Spatial readouts further reveal object identity and attributes such as colour and material at a fine spatial scale. In addition, we extend the “readout carriers” used to express a concept, from a single name token to a set of tokens. This extension helps us better capture and express concept information in intermediate states, and supports subsequent counterfactual experiments on its role in downstream computation. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. The counterfactual experiments indicate that the concept information we access is not merely shown on a “display board”, but also participates in downstream computation and reasoning. In causal reasoning VQA tasks, we perform counterfactual interventions on intermediate concept representations, and find that these interventions can redirect answers to questions requiring multiple steps of reasoning, or influence multiple aspects of downstream reasoning. And we find that these effects generally become stronger as we expand the “readout carriers” using larger concept direction sets. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space based metrics to track correspondence between visual states and language-defined concepts. We also construct a controlled VLM training setting for vision-language alignment, and evaluate these metrics across checkpoints at different stages of training. Our experiments show that our proposed metrics reflect the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than the hidden state cosine baseline. Concept readouts from the same checkpoints further show that concept accessibility improves early in alignment training, whereas reliable selective access develops later. (iv) Shared functions across models. We extend our experiments to VLMs of different sizes from multiple model families ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Gemma Team, 2025 ) . Across these models, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects, despite differences in their internal workspace organisation. Together, these findings provide an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial systems, and open a way to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal alignment. 2 MC-Lens: A Jacobian Lens for Multimodal Concepts In general, a VLM’s output provides only a limited view of its internal processing. For example, a VLM may correctly identify a bicycle in a photograph, but the answer itself does not tell us where the concept of bicycle appears inside the model. Therefore, we develop MC-Lens, a Jacobian-based method inspired by J-Lens ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) , to access concept information from intermediate states in the VLM and to investigate the role of the accessed concepts in downstream computation and reasoning. In this section, we focus on the mathematical formulation of MC-Lens. 2.1 Multimodal Jacobian Lenses In this part, we introduce MC-Lens, a multimodal Jacobian lens that combines V-Lens and L-Lens. V-Lens and L-Lens both apply an averaged Jacobian matrix to measure the effects of intermediate hidden states on the final-layer decoder hidden states in the VLM. V-Lens measures the effect of an intermediate vision encoder state on the final-layer decoder hidden state, while L-Lens measures the corresponding effect of an intermediate language decoder state. For a multimodal input x x , let h ℓ , p m ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ d m h_{\ell,p}^{m}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{m}} denote the intermediate state at layer ℓ \ell and position p p , where m ∈ { E , D , C } m\in\{E,D,C\} marks the vision encoder, the language decoder and the connector, respectively. Here, p p indexes positions in the corresponding patch or token sequence. The connector maps the encoder patches into decoder tokens. The final state h L , q D ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ d D h_{L,q}^{D}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{D}} is the decoder state after the final layer L L at position q q , before the final normalisation. We take the partial derivatives of the final state h L , q D ​ ( x ) h_{L,q}^{D}(x) with respect to the intermediate state h ℓ , p m ​ ( x ) h_{\ell,p}^{m}(x) to measure the effect of a small change δ ​ h ℓ , p m \delta h_{\ell,p}^{m} on the final state. These partial derivatives form the Jacobian matrix J ℓ , p → q m ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ d D × d m J_{\ell,p\rightarrow q}^{m}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{D}\times d^{m}} and give a first-order Taylor approximation of the effect: J ℓ , p → q m ​ ( x ) \displaystyle J_{\ell,p\rightarrow q}^{m}(x) = ∂ h L , q D ​ ( x ) ∂ h ℓ , p m ​ ( x ) , m ∈ { E , D , C } , \displaystyle=\frac{\partial h_{L,q}^{D}(x)}{\partial h_{\ell,p}^{m}(x)},\qquad m\in\{E,D,C\}, (1) δ ​ h L , q D \displaystyle\delta h_{L,q}^{D} ≈ J ℓ , p → q m ​ ( x ) ​ δ ​ h ℓ , p m . \displaystyle\approx J_{\ell,p\rightarrow q}^{m}(x)\,\delta h_{\ell,p}^{m}. (2) Figure 2 : Local Jacobians in a VLM. Squares and circles denote hidden states at patch or token positions. Red and blue dashed arrows show local Jacobians from encoder and decoder states at p p to the same final-layer decoder state at q q . Figure 2 illustrates these local Jacobians for selected encoder and decoder states. However, such a Jacobian matrix mixes two things: the particular use of the intermediate state in the current context, and the general effect it has on later outputs across contexts. J-Lens ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) isolates the general effect by averaging the Jacobian matrices within and across inputs. Specifically, within each input, it sums the Jacobian matrices over the final-layer positions q q and averages over the intermediate positions p p , and it then averages across a corpus of text prompts. In this way, for a given model, we obtain one averaged Jacobian matrix per layer, which serves as the lens for that layer. This uniform averaging strategy in J-Lens ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) suits a language model, since all input positions belong to the same category of text tokens. However, in VLMs, image tokens often greatly outnumber text tokens ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , while text tokens carry the question and other task information and can disproportionately influence the final output ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) . The uniform averaging strategy over the whole sequence would therefore give image positions a larger total weight than text positions in the lens estimate. In addition, in a VLM, the vision encoder processes a sequence of image patches, and the language decoder processes a mixed sequence of image, text and template tokens, so the two lenses need different position sets. We therefore present a unified formulation for V-Lens and L-Lens, and then specify the settings for each lens. We estimate V-Lens and L-Lens from N N VQA examples x i x_{i} , each consisting of an image, a question and the corresponding answer. For each VQA example i i , 𝒫 i \mathcal{P}_{i} is the set of positions p p of the intermediate states, and 𝒬 i \mathcal{Q}_{i} is the set of positions q q of the final-layer decoder states in Equation 1 . The intermediate position set 𝒫 i \mathcal{P}_{i} depends on the lens: for V-Lens it contains the encoder patch positions, and for L-Lens the decoder token positions. We further group 𝒫 i \mathcal{P}_{i} into categories 𝒞 i , c \mathcal{C}_{i,c} , indexed by a category set 𝒦 \mathcal{K} . For V-Lens, 𝒦 \mathcal{K} has a single category containing all patches, and for L-Lens it has three categories: image, text and template tokens. We average within each category and then across categories. This gives each category equal total weight, regardless of how many tokens it contains. The final-layer position set 𝒬 i \mathcal{Q}_{i} is the same for both lenses and contains only the text positions in the decoder. items.raw_text: Probing the “Conscious” Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models Thanks: Here, we use “conscious” to describe functional properties associated with conscious access in global workspace theory. We do not claim that these models possess consciousness or subjective experience. Here, we use “conscious” to describe functional properties associated with conscious access in global workspace theory. We do not claim that these models possess consciousness or subjective experience. Jiahao Huang Jun Wang Jiahao Huang 1 Jun Wang 2† 1 Imperial College London, UK 2 University College London, UK † Corresponding author. Abstract Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information to perform a range of multimodal tasks, but their outputs do not reveal the models’ internal concept representations. In brain science, global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from multiple parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to different specialised processes. In this work, we investigate multimodal concept processing in VLMs in relation to these global workspace functions. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens that combines vision encoder and language decoder lenses. Both lenses map intermediate states into a shared semantic space defined by the decoder’s output vocabulary, allowing us to compare concept accessibility across visual and language processing. MC-Lens also supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. Our experiments address four related aspects. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and can be selectively accessed according to task demands. We extend the “readout carriers” from a single name token to a set of tokens, to better capture and express concept information and support subsequent counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that the concept information we access is not only readable, but also participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space based metrics to track cross-modal concept alignment. In controlled VLM training, these metrics reflect its development more clearly than hidden state cosine. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later in training than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects, despite differences in internal organisation. Together, these findings provide an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial systems, and open a way to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal alignment. Figure 1 : Our proposed Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens). The vision encoder lens (V-Lens) reads object and colour concepts across image patches, while the language decoder lens (L-Lens) tracks how the question changes concept accessibility in the decoder. Both use a shared output vocabulary. Decoder numbers are vocabulary ranks, with smaller values indicating greater concept accessibility. 1 Introduction Vision-language models (VLMs) can effectively integrate visual and textual information to perform a range of multimodal tasks ( Alayrac et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . For example, we can ask a VLM to identify an object in an image or describe its colour, and these questions require the model to extract different information from the same image and integrate it with the textual query. However, although current VLMs can readily answer these questions, their outputs do not reveal their internal concept representations. A VLM can also answer a visual question incorrectly even when the visual information needed to answer it remains readable from its intermediate states ( Fu et al., 2025 ) . Existing interpretability methods aim to identify information in internal states and examine its role in producing model outputs ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; Neo et al., 2025 ; Kaduri et al., 2025 ) . Gurnee et al. (2026) proposed the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens), a Jacobian-based method that provides vocabulary-based readouts of intermediate language-model states. Specifically, it maps the model’s intermediate hidden states into the space of final-layer decoder states via averaged Jacobian matrices, and provides concept directions for counterfactual intervention experiments. Using J-Lens, Gurnee et al. (2026) identify functional and structural properties associated with a global workspace in large language models (LLMs). In brain science, global workspace theory (GWT) ( Baars, 2005 ; Baars and Franklin, 2007 ; Dehaene et al., 1998 ) is an influential theory of consciousness that explains how information from different sources is integrated to support flexible cognition. The core hypothesis of this theory is that information is selected from the multiple parallel processes in the brain, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to different specialised processes. Building on the J-Lens study, we extend this analysis to concept information expressed through different modalities, and processed across the visual and language components of VLMs. In this paper, we introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens that combines a vision encoder lens (V-Lens) and a language decoder lens (L-Lens). V-Lens can access concept information from intermediate vision encoder states before visual information is combined with the text input in the decoder. L-Lens can access concept information from decoder states during the integration of visual and textual inputs, allowing us to examine selective access under different text queries and during autoregressive generation. Both V-Lens and L-Lens map intermediate states into a shared semantic space defined by the decoder’s output vocabulary, so we can compare concept accessibility during multimodal information integration and processing. Figure 1 illustrates these readouts in a visual question answering (VQA) example. We conduct counterfactual experiments using MC-Lens, where we intervene on intermediate state components associated with the accessed concepts and observe the resulting model outputs, to infer the role of these concepts in downstream computation. In addition, we also investigate the functional properties and internal organisation of multimodal concept processing in VLMs in relation to GWT. Specifically, our experiments address four related aspects. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Our experiments show that multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and can be selectively accessed according to task demands. Spatial readouts further reveal object identity and attributes such as colour and material at a fine spatial scale. In addition, we extend the “readout carriers” used to express a concept, from a single name token to a set of tokens. This extension helps us better capture and express concept information in intermediate states, and supports subsequent counterfactual experiments on its role in downstream computation. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. The counterfactual experiments indicate that the concept information we access is not merely shown on a “display board”, but also participates in downstream computation and reasoning. In causal reasoning VQA tasks, we perform counterfactual interventions on intermediate concept representations, and find that these interventions can redirect answers to questions requiring multiple steps of reasoning, or influence multiple aspects of downstream reasoning. And we find that these effects generally become stronger as we expand the “readout carriers” using larger concept direction sets. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space based metrics to track correspondence between visual states and language-defined concepts. We also construct a controlled VLM training setting for vision-language alignment, and evaluate these metrics across checkpoints at different stages of training. Our experiments show that our proposed metrics reflect the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than the hidden state cosine baseline. Concept readouts from the same checkpoints further show that concept accessibility improves early in alignment training, whereas reliable selective access develops later. (iv) Shared functions across models. We extend our experiments to VLMs of different sizes from multiple model families ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Gemma Team, 2025 ) . Across these models, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects, despite differences in their internal workspace organisation. Together, these findings provide an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial systems, and open a way to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal alignment. 2 MC-Lens: A Jacobian Lens for Multimodal Concepts In general, a VLM’s output provides only a limited view of its internal processing. For example, a VLM may correctly identify a bicycle in a photograph, but the answer itself does not tell us where the concept of bicycle appears inside the model. Therefore, we develop MC-Lens, a Jacobian-based method inspired by J-Lens ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) , to access concept information from intermediate states in the VLM and to investigate the role of the accessed concepts in downstream computation and reasoning. In this section, we focus on the mathematical formulation of MC-Lens. 2.1 Multimodal Jacobian Lenses In this part, we introduce MC-Lens, a multimodal Jacobian lens that combines V-Lens and L-Lens. V-Lens and L-Lens both apply an averaged Jacobian matrix to measure the effects of intermediate hidden states on the final-layer decoder hidden states in the VLM. The final state h L , q D ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ d D h_{L,q}^{D}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{D}} is the decoder state after the final layer L L at position q q , before the final normalisation. We take the partial derivatives of the final state h L , q D ​ ( x ) h_{L,q}^{D}(x) with respect to the intermediate state h ℓ , p m ​ ( x ) h_{\ell,p}^{m}(x) to measure the effect of a small change δ ​ h ℓ , p m \delta h_{\ell,p}^{m} on the final state. (2) Figure 2 : Local Jacobians in a VLM. Squares and circles denote hidden states at patch or token positions. Red and blue dashed arrows show local Jacobians from encoder and decoder states at p p to the same final-layer decoder state at q q . Figure 2 illustrates these local Jacobians for selected encoder and decoder states. However, such a Jacobian matrix mixes two things: the particular use of the intermediate state in the current context, and the general effect it has on later outputs across contexts. J-Lens ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) isolates the general effect by averaging the Jacobian matrices within and across inputs. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.26586 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images Authors: Adrià Ciurana Lanau , Harleen Hanspal , Lusine Abrahamyan , Emilio Tylson Baixauli , Yu Cao , Danai Triantafyllidou , Stefano Zorzi , Gustavo Zanoni Felipe , Peter Griger , Stefan Sietzen , Petru-Daniel Tudosiu View a PDF of the paper titled ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images, by Adri\`a Ciurana Lanau and 10 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs $19.1\times$ faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade. items.content: ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images Adrià Ciurana Lanau Affiliation: Canva Email: adria@canva.com Harleen Hanspal Affiliation: Canva Email: hhanspal@canva.com Lusine Abrahamyan Affiliation: Canva Email: lusine@canva.com Emilio Tylson Baixauli Affiliation: Canva Email: emilio@canva.com Yu Cao Affiliation: Queen Mary University of London Email: danai@canva.com Danai Triantafyllidou Affiliation: Canva Email: szorzi@canva.com Stefano Zorzi Affiliation: Canva Email: gzanoni@canva.com Gustavo Zanoni Felipe Affiliation: Universidade Estadual de Maringá Email: petergriger@canva.com Peter Griger Affiliation: Canva Email: stefan@canva.com Stefan Sietzen Affiliation: Canva Email: ptudosiu@canva.com Petru-Daniel Tudosiu Affiliation: Canva Abstract Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For N N layers, the representation contains H ​ W + N HW+N tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with N ​ H ​ W NHW for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs 19.1 × 19.1\times faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade. Figure 1 : ProtoDiffusion across its conditioning regimes. (a) Box-guided image-to-design: the input composite, with supplied element boxes, is decomposed into editable RGBA layers. (b) Image-to-design: the same decomposition from the composite alone, without boxes. (c) Text-to-design: generation of a layered design from a text prompt. Each group shows the composite at left and the recovered layers at right. 1 Introduction Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA elements: text, shapes, cutouts, and photographs over a background. Blending these layers produces an alpha-composited image . Keeping these elements separate enables selection, movement, and reuse after generation. Standard text-to-image diffusion [ 24 ] instead produces a flattened raster, in which those editing units are entangled. Layered models already generate coherent transparent elements, but they share two constraints. First, every layer has its own spatial latent: a full-canvas grid in Qwen-Image-Layered (QIL) [ 34 ] and a region grid in MRT [ 27 ] . The sequence processed by the denoiser, and with it compute and memory, therefore grows with the number and extent of layers (Section 4.5 ). Second, structure is decided before content: QIL takes a requested layer count, and MRT a layout that is supplied or estimated beforehand, so the number of layers, and in MRT their placement, is fixed before denoising begins. The two are linked: deciding structure jointly with content means denoising many candidate layers, which is costly when each one is a spatial grid. The use of a prior layout is analogous to two-stage instance segmentation (e.g., Mask R-CNN [ 7 ] ): propose regions, then predict instances. As in that setting, the second stage cannot revise what the first provides: a missing or misplaced region is not corrected during layer generation, and the layout must come from a separate model or the user. Inspired by the shared prototype masks and per-instance coefficients in YOLACT [ 2 ] , we instead factorize a design into a shared spatial grid and layer-specific candidates, extending the idea to joint generation and nonlinear decoding of RGBA layers. We propose a token-per-layer representation. ProtoVAE jointly encodes the layer stack into a shared spatial grid (the prototype ) and one candidate vector per layer, including the background. Each candidate summarizes its layer in the context of the full composition and conditions the decoder to reconstruct the corresponding RGBA layer from the shared grid (Figure 2 ). ProtoDiffusion learns a diffusion model over this factorization. A pretrained image-transformer stream processes the shared grid, while a dedicated candidate stream exchanges information with it through bidirectional cross-attention (Figure 3 ). The same model serves different tasks by changing the conditioning: image-to-design conditions on the encoded alpha-composited image, and text-to-design on a prompt. Boxes guide candidates when available. The model denoises a fixed set of candidate slots and leaves unneeded ones empty. It thus determines the number of layers and, when no boxes are given, their layout, requiring neither as input. Figure 1 illustrates image-to-design with and without boxes and text-to-design generation. Specifically, our contributions are: 1. Compact latent representation. A token-per-layer factorization, ProtoVAE, represents an RGBA design with H ​ W + N HW+N tokens before packing for N N layers, versus N ⋅ H ​ W N\!\cdot\!HW for full-grid-per-layer representations. Each additional layer costs one candidate vector rather than a spatial grid. Section 3.3 derives the resulting denoiser scaling separately from measured system-level speedups. 2. Joint denoising of design context and elements. A two-stream diffusion architecture couples the shared prototype grid and layer candidates through bidirectional cross-attention, jointly modeling composition and layer content. 3. Unified generation and decomposition. A single model supports image-to-design with or without bounding boxes and text-to-design generation through changes in conditioning. Activity-based candidate selection recovers a variable number of layers within a fixed capacity. 2 Related Work Layered image generation and decomposition. Layered representations allow individual elements of an image to be edited and reused. LayerDiffuse [ 35 ] introduces latent transparency, enabling pretrained diffusion models to generate transparent images and multiple interacting layers. Qwen-Image-Layered [ 34 ] encodes each RGBA layer as a spatial latent grid and models interactions across layers with a variable-length diffusion transformer. Its decomposition interface takes an image and a requested layer count, without requiring bounding boxes. MRT [ 27 ] uses region-based spatial latents and a masked diffusion formulation for text-to-layer generation, image decomposition, and layer editing. Its layer generator receives a layout specifying the regions and their ordering. PSDiffusion [ 12 ] generates multiple layers simultaneously, with global interactions that coordinate their layout and appearance. For image decomposition, LayerD [ 26 ] iteratively extracts unoccluded foreground layers through matting and completes the remaining background through inpainting. RevealLayer [ 28 ] focuses on natural-image decomposition, including occluded content and layer separation, and introduces RevealLayerBench. LayeringDiff [ 16 ] first generates a composite image and then uses generative priors to disassemble it into foreground and background layers. For iterative editing, SLEDGE [ 17 ] studies sequences of instruction-guided layered edits, while Wu et al. [ 32 ] investigate the effect of synthetic layered training data on design decomposition. ProtoVAE addresses the spatial cost of these representations by sharing one prototype across layers and adding only one token per layer, instead of a full or regional grid. Graphic design and layout generation. COLE [ 15 ] uses hierarchical design planning and generation, while Desigen [ 30 ] predicts layouts conditioned on generated backgrounds. LayoutDM [ 13 ] and LayoutGPT [ 6 ] generate layouts through discrete diffusion and language models, respectively. Our framework accepts optional boxes and otherwise jointly models spatial structure and layer content from text or image conditioning. Figure 2 : ProtoVAE: shared grid, one candidate per layer. (a) The frozen QIL encoder maps each RGBA layer to a spatial latent; a layer-wise transformer jointly processes the projected layer maps with a learned layer token, whose output parameterizes the shared prototype posterior, giving H ​ W + N HW+N tokens per design before backbone-specific packing. (b) Candidate extraction maps each contextualized layer map to a candidate posterior: a crop around the alpha-derived box, a CNN with average pooling, and a cross-attention distribution extractor. (c) Each candidate modulates the shared prototype decoder through AdaLN-Zero, and the jointly trained QIL decoder reconstructs its RGBA layer. Snowflakes mark frozen modules and flames mark trainable modules. Feature grids and outputs are schematic. Latent generative representations. We build on latent diffusion [ 24 ] , transformer denoisers [ 23 ] , and flow matching [ 19 ] to jointly model the shared prototype and per-layer candidates. The supplementary material discusses object-centric representations and reconstruction objectives. 3 Method We adopt a two-stage training procedure: ProtoVAE learns a latent representation of layered designs, and ProtoDiffusion is subsequently trained in this latent space. Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the representation and denoising architecture, respectively. Throughout, H H and W W denote the latent spatial dimensions, C C the number of ProtoVAE latent channels, N N the number of design layers (including the background), and M M the number of diffusion slots. 3.1 ProtoVAE: Shared Spatial Context and Layer Identity Encoding. Given an ordered design { x i } i = 1 N \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} including its background, the frozen QIL VAE encoder maps each RGBA layer to a spatial latent, which is projected to hidden width D D . The projected layer maps are jointly processed by LayerSquasher , a layer-wise vision transformer that alternates spatial self-attention within each layer ( x ​ y xy ) with self-attention across layers ( z z ). This joint processing provides shared spatial context for constructing the prototype and per-layer candidates. A learned token z ℓ ∈ ℝ D z_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is broadcast into an additional spatial layer of size D × H × W D\times H\times W and jointly processed with the N N projected layer maps. Its output aggregates information from the entire design and parameterizes the shared prototype posterior. The remaining N N outputs are pooled to parameterize candidate posteriors, each representing a layer in the context of the full design. Specifically, this pooling operation crops each contextualized layer feature map to a region around its alpha-derived bounding box and resizes it. A small CNN followed by global average pooling summarizes the region into a vector. An attention-based distribution extractor refines this vector using prototype context and box features. The boxes are derived from observed layers during encoding; they are not externally supplied generation-time layouts. The resulting diagonal-Gaussian posteriors define the prototype p ∈ ℝ C × H × W p\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} and candidates c i ∈ ℝ C c_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} , with C = 128 C=128 . Decoding. Each candidate conditions the shared prototype decoder through AdaLN-Zero [ 23 ] , producing a spatial latent for that layer; the QIL decoder converts it to RGBA pixels. During ProtoVAE training, the QIL encoder remains frozen, while LayerSquasher, the pooling operator, the prototype decoder, and the QIL decoder are trained jointly. This fine-tuning adapts the QIL decoder to design layers with small elements, fine details, and large transparent regions; the adapted decoder is retained for subsequent reconstruction and generation. All candidates therefore share spatial context, but each selects its own reconstruction. The supplementary material gives the encoder and decoder details, including candidate refinement and training implementation. Figure 3 : ProtoDiffusion: conditioning, noising, and joint denoising. Image and text conditioning remain clean while the shared prototype and M M candidate slots are jointly denoised through interacting streams. Training interpolates the clean state z 0 z_{0} and Gaussian noise z 1 z_{1} as z t = ( 1 − t ) ​ z 0 + t ​ z 1 z_{t}=(1-t)z_{0}+tz_{1} ; generation starts at z 1 z_{1} . Optional bounding boxes provide spatial guidance. Activity-based selection retains N ≤ M N\leq M candidates, which are decoded with the predicted clean prototype p ^ \hat{p} into RGBA layers. The state contains H ​ W + M HW+M tokens before backbone-specific packing. Snowflakes and flames indicate frozen and trainable modules during diffusion training. Output thumbnails are schematic. Training objectives. We train ProtoVAE with pixel- and latent-space reconstruction losses, KL regularization of the prototype and candidate posteriors, prototype alignment, and adversarial supervision. Reconstruction supervises complete RGBA layers, including occluded content. Adversarial supervision uses a discriminator on stacked layer latents and a PatchGAN [ 14 ] on alpha-composited local crops. The supplementary material provides further objective and training details. Prototype alignment. Inspired by DC-Gen [ 8 ] , an alignment module encourages agreement between features of the shared prototype and the frozen QIL encoding of the composited image. This regularizes shared spatial context, while per-layer reconstruction supervises hidden content; alignment does not require the prototype to equal the composite latent. Overlap and leakage weighting. We increase pixel- and latent-space reconstruction weights in regions of inter-layer overlap to emphasize occluded content. Just outside each layer’s support, alpha-only weighting penalizes leakage without constraining invisible RGB. 3.2 Joint Prototype and Candidate Diffusion The transformer adapts FLUX.2-Klein-4B [ 1 ] to the ProtoVAE prototype–candidate latent space. Prototype tokens use the backbone’s image self-attention and spatial RoPE [ 25 ] . Candidates have a dedicated self-attention stream with AdaLN-Zero timestep conditioning. Bidirectional cross-attention synchronizes the streams every k = 4 k=4 blocks, allowing layer identities and spatial context to interact during denoising. Conditioning and occupancy. Training slots follow increasing stacking level ( z z -layer), then top-to-bottom and left-to-right box-center order within each level. Generated layers are alpha-composited in retained slot order. For image-to-design, the alpha-composited input image is encoded directly by the frozen QIL encoder, without running the layered-input ProtoVAE encoder. For text-to-design, the prototype and M M candidate slots are sampled jointly from noise under text conditioning. Candidate conditioning and occupancy are handled as follows: • With boxes (layout-guided): box-derived RoPE and Fourier box embeddings provide spatial conditioning. • Without boxes: candidate-ID RoPE identifies the slots, and box embeddings are zeroed; no external layout is supplied. • Layer count: unused slots are trained toward an empty state. For each denoised candidate vector c ~ i \tilde{c}_{i} , we compute a i = | mean ⁡ ( c ~ i ) | + std ⁡ ( c ~ i ) a_{i}=|\operatorname{mean}(\tilde{c}_{i})|+\operatorname{std}(\tilde{c}_{i}) across channels and retain slots with a i > θ a_{i}>\theta . The highest-scoring slot is always retained, yielding 1 ≤ N ≤ M 1\leq N\leq M . We set the default candidate capacity to M = 50 M=50 . Occupancy-based selection removes the need to request an exact count, but retains a capacity setting and an occupancy threshold. Even when boxes specify a count, the current implementation still denoises M M slots. Autoregressive candidate generation with a learned stopping criterion could remove this fixed-slot constraint; we leave this extension to future work. The supplementary material reports a threshold-calibration study on 1,954 samples. Diffusion training. We use flow matching with z t = ( 1 − t ) ​ z 0 + t ​ ϵ z_{t}=(1-t)z_{0}+t\epsilon , where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) , and velocity target ϵ − z 0 \epsilon-z_{0} . The training objective is ℒ = ℒ p + λ c ​ ℒ c + λ layer ​ ( ℒ QIL ​ - ​ L1 + λ sep ​ ℒ sep ) . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{p}+\lambda_{c}\mathcal{L}_{c}+\lambda_{\mathrm{layer}}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QIL\text{-}L1}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}\bigr). Here, ℒ p \mathcal{L}_{p} and ℒ c \mathcal{L}_{c} are mean squared velocity errors, normalized separately within the prototype and candidate streams. Real and empty candidate slots are also reduced separately, so candidate supervision does not scale with the number of padding slots. For layered supervision, the predicted clean prototype and candidates are decoded through the frozen ProtoVAE decoder into per-layer QIL latents, retaining gradients with respect to the predicted prototype and candidates. The reconstruction term ℒ QIL ​ - ​ L1 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QIL\text{-}L1}} measures weighted L 1 L_{1} error against the target latents, emphasizing occluded regions and excluding padding layers. Inspired by RevealLayer [ 28 ] , ℒ sep \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}} contrasts each predicted layer with its own target and other layers. The comparison uses corresponding canvas positions, without pooling or crop recentering. The supplementary material provides the loss definitions, weighting schemes, and reduction details. 3.3 Representation Cost Before backbone-specific packing, a design’s latent representation has L ProtoVAE = H ​ W + N , L diffusion = H ​ W + M . L_{\mathrm{ProtoVAE}}=HW+N,\qquad L_{\mathrm{diffusion}}=HW+M. A full-grid-per-layer representation has N ​ H ​ W NHW tokens; region grids instead incur an area-dependent cost. After packing, let S S be the spatial token count per grid. At fixed depth, hidden widths, and conditioning length, our two-stream attention costs O ⁡ ( S 2 + M 2 + S ​ M ) O(S^{2}+M^{2}+SM) , including cross-stream exchange, versus O ⁡ ( ( N ​ S ) 2 ) O((NS)^{2}) for joint dense attention over N N full grids. Token-wise projections and MLPs process S + M S+M rather than N ​ S NS tokens. Thus increasing layer capacity adds candidate tokens instead of spatial grids. With M M fixed, retaining more layers does not lengthen denoising; RGBA decoding still scales with output count. Figure 6 complements this analysis with system-level latency and memory measurements, which also reflect differences in backbone, conditioning, and execution. The supplementary material provides the full complexity analysis. 4 Experiments We evaluate reconstruction fidelity, image-to-design decomposition, text-to-design generation, and computational efficiency. Figure 4 : Qualitative image-to-design decomposition without bounding boxes on Crello inputs. Columns: the input composite and the layers recovered by ProtoDiffusion, QIL, and LayerD, shown over a checkerboard. Examples are selected and illustrative, not a systematic comparison. Figure 5 : Qualitative box-guided image-to-design decomposition on Crello inputs. Columns: the input composite with the supplied element boxes overlaid, and the background and layers recovered by ProtoDiffusion and CLD, shown over a checkerboard. Examples are selected and illustrative, not a systematic comparison. 4.1 Experimental Setup Training datasets. We train on layered graphic designs and PrismLayersPro [ 4 ] compositions, augmented with synthetic compositions built from COYO [ 3 ] images and graphic elements. We also use RevealLayer [ 28 ] data and its foreground elements, together with additional synthetic examples generated using FLUX and LanPaint [ 37 ] . ProtoVAE is trained on this mixture with random layer permutations. ProtoDiffusion uses the same data for image-to-design training with and without bounding boxes. For text-to-design, the final training stage uses a curated subset that excludes fully synthetic compositions to preserve aesthetics. Evaluation datasets. We evaluate reconstruction and image-to-design decomposition on Crello [ 33 ] , following the LayerD evaluation split for decomposition [ 26 ] . Training schedule. To adapt the pretrained image backbone, we first train the newly introduced candidate, cross-attention, and box-conditioning modules, then progressively unfreeze the backbone. The supplementary material summarizes the training setup. Baselines. We compare image-to-design decomposition with QIL [ 34 ] , LayerD [ 26 ] , and CLD [ 21 ] , and computational efficiency with QIL and MRT [ 27 ] . 4.2 Reconstruction Fidelity Table 1: RGBA reconstruction on 1,000 held-out Crello designs (10,036 layers) at 1024 pixels on the longest axis. Joint indicates shared compression of the layer stack. PSNR, SSIM [ 29 ] , and LPIPS [ 36 ] average nine backgrounds, then layers and designs; rFID [ 9 ] averages background-specific distribution scores. QIL + adapted decoder is an independent-layer reference. Best values overall are bold; best joint-model values are underlined. The bold row denotes our best joint reconstruction model. Graphic design and layout generation. COLE [ 15 ] uses hierarchical design planning and generation, while Desigen [ 30 ] predicts layouts conditioned on generated backgrounds. LayoutDM [ 13 ] and LayoutGPT [ 6 ] generate layouts through discrete diffusion and language models, respectively. Our framework accepts optional boxes and otherwise jointly models spatial structure and layer content from text or image conditioning. Figure 2 : ProtoVAE: shared grid, one candidate per layer. (a) The frozen QIL encoder maps each RGBA layer to a spatial latent; a layer-wise transformer jointly processes the projected layer maps with a learned layer token, whose output parameterizes the shared prototype posterior, giving H ​ W + N HW+N tokens per design before backbone-specific packing. (b) Candidate extraction maps each contextualized layer map to a candidate posterior: a crop around the alpha-derived box, a CNN with average pooling, and a cross-attention distribution extractor. (c) Each candidate modulates the shared prototype decoder through AdaLN-Zero, and the jointly trained QIL decoder reconstructs its RGBA layer. Snowflakes mark frozen modules and flames mark trainable modules. Feature grids and outputs are schematic. Latent generative representations. We build on latent diffusion [ 24 ] , transformer denoisers [ 23 ] , and flow matching [ 19 ] to jointly model the shared prototype and per-layer candidates. The supplementary material discusses object-centric representations and reconstruction objectives. 3 Method We adopt a two-stage training procedure: ProtoVAE learns a latent representation of layered designs, and ProtoDiffusion is subsequently trained in this latent space. Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the representation and denoising architecture, respectively. Throughout, H H and W W denote the latent spatial dimensions, C C the number of ProtoVAE latent channels, N N the number of design layers (including the background), and M M the number of diffusion slots. 3.1 ProtoVAE: Shared Spatial Context and Layer Identity Encoding. Given an ordered design { x i } i = 1 N \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} including its background, the frozen QIL VAE encoder maps each RGBA layer to a spatial latent, which is projected to hidden width D D . The projected layer maps are jointly processed by LayerSquasher , a layer-wise vision transformer that alternates spatial self-attention within each layer ( x ​ y xy ) with self-attention across layers ( z z ). This joint processing provides shared spatial context for constructing the prototype and per-layer candidates. A learned token z ℓ ∈ ℝ D z_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is broadcast into an additional spatial layer of size D × H × W D\times H\times W and jointly processed with the N N projected layer maps. Its output aggregates information from the entire design and parameterizes the shared prototype posterior. The remaining N N outputs are pooled to parameterize candidate posteriors, each representing a layer in the context of the full design. Specifically, this pooling operation crops each contextualized layer feature map to a region around its alpha-derived bounding box and resizes it. A small CNN followed by global average pooling summarizes the region into a vector. An attention-based distribution extractor refines this vector using prototype context and box features. The boxes are derived from observed layers during encoding; they are not externally supplied generation-time layouts. The resulting diagonal-Gaussian posteriors define the prototype p ∈ ℝ C × H × W p\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} and candidates c i ∈ ℝ C c_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} , with C = 128 C=128 . Decoding. Each candidate conditions the shared prototype decoder through AdaLN-Zero [ 23 ] , producing a spatial latent for that layer; the QIL decoder converts it to RGBA pixels. During ProtoVAE training, the QIL encoder remains frozen, while LayerSquasher, the pooling operator, the prototype decoder, and the QIL decoder are trained jointly. This fine-tuning adapts the QIL decoder to design layers with small elements, fine details, and large transparent regions; the adapted decoder is retained for subsequent reconstruction and generation. All candidates therefore share spatial context, but each selects its own reconstruction. The supplementary material gives the encoder and decoder details, including candidate refinement and training implementation. Figure 3 : ProtoDiffusion: conditioning, noising, and joint denoising. Image and text conditioning remain clean while the shared prototype and M M candidate slots are jointly denoised through interacting streams. Training interpolates the clean state z 0 z_{0} and Gaussian noise z 1 z_{1} as z t = ( 1 − t ) ​ z 0 + t ​ z 1 z_{t}=(1-t)z_{0}+tz_{1} ; generation starts at z 1 z_{1} . Optional bounding boxes provide spatial guidance. Activity-based selection retains N ≤ M N\leq M candidates, which are decoded with the predicted clean prototype p ^ \hat{p} into RGBA layers. The state contains H ​ W + M HW+M tokens before backbone-specific packing. Snowflakes and flames indicate frozen and trainable modules during diffusion training. Output thumbnails are schematic. Training objectives. We train ProtoVAE with pixel- and latent-space reconstruction losses, KL regularization of the prototype and candidate posteriors, prototype alignment, and adversarial supervision. Reconstruction supervises complete RGBA layers, including occluded content. Adversarial supervision uses a discriminator on stacked layer latents and a PatchGAN [ 14 ] on alpha-composited local crops. The supplementary material provides further objective and training details. Prototype alignment. Inspired by DC-Gen [ 8 ] , an alignment module encourages agreement between features of the shared prototype and the frozen QIL encoding of the composited image. This regularizes shared spatial context, while per-layer reconstruction supervises hidden content; alignment does not require the prototype to equal the composite latent. Overlap and leakage weighting. We increase pixel- and latent-space reconstruction weights in regions of inter-layer overlap to emphasize occluded content. Just outside each layer’s support, alpha-only weighting penalizes leakage without constraining invisible RGB. 3.2 Joint Prototype and Candidate Diffusion The transformer adapts FLUX.2-Klein-4B [ 1 ] to the ProtoVAE prototype–candidate latent space. Prototype tokens use the backbone’s image self-attention and spatial RoPE [ 25 ] . Candidates have a dedicated self-attention stream with AdaLN-Zero timestep conditioning. Bidirectional cross-attention synchronizes the streams every k = 4 k=4 blocks, allowing layer identities and spatial context to interact during denoising. Conditioning and occupancy. Training slots follow increasing stacking level ( z z -layer), then top-to-bottom and left-to-right box-center order within each level. Generated layers are alpha-composited in retained slot order. For image-to-design, the alpha-composited input image is encoded directly by the frozen QIL encoder, without running the layered-input ProtoVAE encoder. For text-to-design, the prototype and M M candidate slots are sampled jointly from noise under text conditioning. Candidate conditioning and occupancy are handled as follows: • With boxes (layout-guided): box-derived RoPE and Fourier box embeddings provide spatial conditioning. • Without boxes: candidate-ID RoPE identifies the slots, and box embeddings are zeroed; no external layout is supplied. • Layer count: unused slots are trained toward an empty state. For each denoised candidate vector c ~ i \tilde{c}_{i} , we compute a i = | mean ⁡ ( c ~ i ) | + std ⁡ ( c ~ i ) a_{i}=|\operatorname{mean}(\tilde{c}_{i})|+\operatorname{std}(\tilde{c}_{i}) across channels and retain slots with a i > θ a_{i}>\theta . The highest-scoring slot is always retained, yielding 1 ≤ N ≤ M 1\leq N\leq M . We set the default candidate capacity to M = 50 M=50 . Occupancy-based selection removes the need to request an exact count, but retains a capacity setting and an occupancy threshold. Even when boxes specify a count, the current implementation still denoises M M slots. Autoregressive candidate generation with a learned stopping criterion could remove this fixed-slot constraint; we leave this extension to future work. The supplementary material reports a threshold-calibration study on 1,954 samples. Diffusion training. We use flow matching with z t = ( 1 − t ) ​ z 0 + t ​ ϵ z_{t}=(1-t)z_{0}+t\epsilon , where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) , and velocity target ϵ − z 0 \epsilon-z_{0} . The training objective is ℒ = ℒ p + λ c ​ ℒ c + λ layer ​ ( ℒ QIL ​ - ​ L1 + λ sep ​ ℒ sep ) . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{p}+\lambda_{c}\mathcal{L}_{c}+\lambda_{\mathrm{layer}}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QIL\text{-}L1}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}\bigr). Here, ℒ p \mathcal{L}_{p} and ℒ c \mathcal{L}_{c} are mean squared velocity errors, normalized separately within the prototype and candidate streams. Real and empty candidate slots are also reduced separately, so candidate supervision does not scale with the number of padding slots. For layered supervision, the predicted clean prototype and candidates are decoded through the frozen ProtoVAE decoder into per-layer QIL latents, retaining gradients with respect to the predicted prototype and candidates. The reconstruction term ℒ QIL ​ - ​ L1 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{QIL\text{-}L1}} measures weighted L 1 L_{1} error against the target latents, emphasizing occluded regions and excluding padding layers. Inspired by RevealLayer [ 28 ] , ℒ sep \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}} contrasts each predicted layer with its own target and other layers. The comparison uses corresponding canvas positions, without pooling or crop recentering. The supplementary material provides the loss definitions, weighting schemes, and reduction details. 3.3 Representation Cost Before backbone-specific packing, a design’s latent representation has L ProtoVAE = H ​ W + N , L diffusion = H ​ W + M . L_{\mathrm{ProtoVAE}}=HW+N,\qquad L_{\mathrm{diffusion}}=HW+M. A full-grid-per-layer representation has N ​ H ​ W NHW tokens; region grids instead incur an area-dependent cost. After packing, let S S be the spatial token count per grid. At fixed depth, hidden widths, and conditioning length, our two-stream attention costs O ⁡ ( S 2 + M 2 + S ​ M ) O(S^{2}+M^{2}+SM) , including cross-stream exchange, versus O ⁡ ( ( N ​ S ) 2 ) O((NS)^{2}) for joint dense attention over N N full grids. Token-wise projections and MLPs process S + M S+M rather than N ​ S NS tokens. Thus increasing layer capacity adds candidate tokens instead of spatial grids. With M M fixed, retaining more layers does not lengthen denoising; RGBA decoding still scales with output count. Figure 6 complements this analysis with system-level latency and memory measurements, which also reflect differences in backbone, conditioning, and execution. The supplementary material provides the full complexity analysis. 4 Experiments We evaluate reconstruction fidelity, image-to-design decomposition, text-to-design generation, and computational efficiency. Figure 4 : Qualitative image-to-design decomposition without bounding boxes on Crello inputs. Columns: the input composite and the layers recovered by ProtoDiffusion, QIL, and LayerD, shown over a checkerboard. Examples are selected and illustrative, not a systematic comparison. Figure 5 : Qualitative box-guided image-to-design decomposition on Crello inputs. Columns: the input composite with the supplied element boxes overlaid, and the background and layers recovered by ProtoDiffusion and CLD, shown over a checkerboard. Examples are selected and illustrative, not a systematic comparison. 4.1 Experimental Setup Training datasets. We train on layered graphic designs and PrismLayersPro [ 4 ] compositions, augmented with synthetic compositions built from COYO [ 3 ] images and graphic elements. We also use RevealLayer [ 28 ] data and its foreground elements, together with additional synthetic examples generated using FLUX and LanPaint [ 37 ] . ProtoVAE is trained on this mixture with random layer permutations. ProtoDiffusion uses the same data for image-to-design training with and without bounding boxes. For text-to-design, the final training stage uses a curated subset that excludes fully synthetic compositions to preserve aesthetics. Evaluation datasets. We evaluate reconstruction and image-to-design decomposition on Crello [ 33 ] , following the LayerD evaluation split for decomposition [ 26 ] . Training schedule. To adapt the pretrained image backbone, we first train the newly introduced candidate, cross-attention, and box-conditioning modules, then progressively unfreeze the backbone. The supplementary material summarizes the training setup. Baselines. We compare image-to-design decomposition with QIL [ 34 ] , LayerD [ 26 ] , and CLD [ 21 ] , and computational efficiency with QIL and MRT [ 27 ] . 4.2 Reconstruction Fidelity Table 1: RGBA reconstruction on 1,000 held-out Crello designs (10,036 layers) at 1024 pixels on the longest axis. Joint indicates shared compression of the layer stack. PSNR, SSIM [ 29 ] , and LPIPS [ 36 ] average nine backgrounds, then layers and designs; rFID [ 9 ] averages background-specific distribution scores. QIL + adapted decoder is an independent-layer reference. Best values overall are bold; best joint-model values are underlined. The bold row denotes our best joint reconstruction model. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.26557 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models Authors: Jinzhe Li , Qi Wang , Dandan Guo , Li Liu , Yuan Wu , Yi Chang View a PDF of the paper titled MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models, by Jinzhe Li and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: When multimodal decision models determine actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judgments, their reliability depends on preserving semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguishing information consistent with task evidence from information that conflicts with it. Existing evaluations study decision-interface biases and multimodal model behavior in separate settings, leaving no common protocol to compare multimodal decision models with their backbones on practical tasks. We introduce \textbf{MM-SystemOneBias}, which evaluates 13 models on 5,323 original instances from nine public datasets and 11 task scenarios using six paired interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image--text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Across seven matched decision-model--backbone pairs, decision models are more stable under option-label, irrelevant-information, and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs; six pairs also show lower option-order flip rates. They incur smaller accuracy losses under incorrect external judgments in all seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct external judgments and show less favorable accuracy changes under consistent descriptions. Among pairs with unchanged semantic decisions, mean absolute changes in answer probabilities range from 4.56 to 11.55 percentage points, revealing input effects that accuracy alone misses. items.summary: MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models Jinzhe Li Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: International Center of Future Science, Jilin University Qi Wang Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Dandan Guo Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) Li Liu Affiliation: School of Big Data and Software Engineering, Chongqing University{jinzhe25}@mails.jlu.edu.cn, dcsliuli@cqu.edu.cn, {qiwang, guodandan, yuanwu, yichang}@jlu.edu.cn Yuan Wu † † thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Yi Chang Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: Engineering Research Center of Knowledge-Driven Human-Machine Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: International Center of Future Science, Jilin University Abstract W
items.content: MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models Jinzhe Li Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: International Center of Future Science, Jilin University Qi Wang Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Dandan Guo Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) Li Liu Affiliation: School of Big Data and Software Engineering, Chongqing University{jinzhe25}@mails.jlu.edu.cn, dcsliuli@cqu.edu.cn, {qiwang, guodandan, yuanwu, yichang}@jlu.edu.cn Yuan Wu † † thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Yi Chang Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: Engineering Research Center of Knowledge-Driven Human-Machine Intelligence, Jilin University Affiliation: International Center of Future Science, Jilin University Abstract When multimodal decision models determine actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judgments, their reliability depends on preserving semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguishing information consistent with task evidence from information that conflicts with it. Existing evaluations study decision-interface biases and multimodal model behavior in separate settings, leaving no common protocol to compare multimodal decision models with their backbones on practical tasks. We introduce MM-SystemOneBias , which evaluates 13 models on 5,323 original instances from nine public datasets and 11 task scenarios using six paired interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image–text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Across seven matched decision-model–backbone pairs, decision models are more stable under option-label, irrelevant-information, and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs; six pairs also show lower option-order flip rates. They incur smaller accuracy losses under incorrect external judgments in all seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct external judgments and show less favorable accuracy changes under consistent descriptions. Among pairs with unchanged semantic decisions, mean absolute changes in answer probabilities range from 4.56 to 11.55 percentage points, revealing input effects that accuracy alone misses. 1 Introduction Recent advances in System One models have made typed decisions over finite answer spaces practical for structured tasks ( Deußer et al., 2026 ; Geuter et al., 2026 ) . Multimodal systems extend this interface to applications such as web interaction and image assessment ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Yue et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2023 ) , where a model decision can determine an action, a moderation outcome, or a quality judgment. Their reliability therefore matters beyond answer accuracy on a fixed presentation. Figure 1: Intervention sensitivity across multimodal decision models and general-purpose vision-language models. Axes show semantic flip rate, error introduction rate, or mean absolute grade shift for the six intervention types. Decision models are generally less sensitive to option and rating-scale interventions, while sensitivity to external judgments and image–text descriptions varies across models. A reliable multimodal decision model should preserve its semantic answer when option order changes. Its decision should also remain stable when candidate labels or rating values change. It should respond appropriately to external judgments and image–text descriptions, and irrelevant information should not alter its answer. These requirements are distinct from general multimodal capability: a model may recognize the relevant visual content yet change its decision under an intervention. However, existing evaluations leave this behavior incompletely characterized. Studies of typed and multiple-choice decision models examine position, label, and scale biases ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Azizi et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2023a ; Zhao et al., 2021 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Liusie et al., 2023 ) , while multimodal bias studies mainly evaluate general-purpose models or MLLM-as-a-Judge systems under open-ended generation, question answering, or scoring ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Lai and Huang, 2026 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2025 ) . These settings differ from finite semantic decisions on practical multimodal tasks, and existing work does not provide a common protocol for comparing decision models with their corresponding general-purpose backbones. To address this gap, we introduce MM-SystemOneBias , a systematic benchmark for bias in multimodal decision models. It covers 5,323 original instances from 9 public datasets and 11 task scenarios, evaluates 8 decision models and 5 general-purpose vision-language models, and applies six controlled interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image–text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Paired comparisons measure semantic decisions, task accuracy, and probabilities assigned to answers. Seven decision-model–backbone pairs support matched comparisons across the five backbones. Across the six bias types, the decision models show heterogeneous sensitivity, with individual models exhibiting large changes under particular interventions (Figure 1 ). Across matched pairs, decision models have lower flip rates under option-label and irrelevant-information interventions and smaller rating-scale shifts in all seven pairs; option-order flip rates are lower in six. They also lose less accuracy under incorrect external judgments in all seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct judgments and show less favorable accuracy changes under consistent descriptions. In image–text tasks, conflicting descriptions can redirect correct decisions even when a model rejects the false claim in an isolated probe; an image-first instruction reduces this task error. The sources cover GUI interaction, robot actions and states, document type classification, image safety moderation, industrial anomaly detection, image-grounded response preference, and generated-image quality: Multimodal-Mind2Web ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) , AgentRewardBench ( Lù et al., 2025 ) , Robo2VLM-1 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , RVL-CDIP ( Harley et al., 2015 ) , LlavaGuard ( Helff et al., 2024 ) , MVTec AD ( Bergmann et al., 2019 ) , VL-RewardBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) , HPDv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , and AGIQA-3K ( Li et al., 2024a ) . We form each original instance from a source instance’s images, task text, and annotation. Choice tasks use source options when available; otherwise, we pair the correct target with incorrect alternatives. Yes/no answers follow task outcomes, policy annotations, or defect labels. For image quality, dataset-wide MOS quantiles define ordered reference grades and their corresponding acceptability labels. A source instance that supports multiple interfaces retains a shared identity across its derived instances. Appendix C details these conversions, and Table 6 maps each source to its tasks and sampling unit. Sampling and Test-Set Composition. We sample from native test partitions where available and select shuffled source groups for the remaining datasets. The sample preserves both outcomes where relevant and all five image-quality grades, while balancing correct-answer positions within choice tasks. Related trajectories, queries, prompts, and shared images remain together. Appendix C.3 specifies the grouping units and quotas; Appendix E reports the retained composition. Intervention Construction. Each intervened instance is paired with an original instance. Its construction changes one input factor while preserving the task and semantic answer mapping. The six bias types define the factor changed in each pair: Option order. We reorder the candidates and move their display labels with them, leaving candidate content and semantic identity unchanged. Option label. We replace the candidate labels while leaving candidate content, order, and semantic identity unchanged. External judgment. We append a fixed-template conclusion and vary both its agreement with the reference answer and its attributed source or tone. Image–text description. We add a pair of descriptions: one supported by the task-relevant visual evidence and one that contradicts it. Irrelevant information. We append background items from other source instances in the same evaluation pool and vary how many appear in the input. Rating scale. We change the numbers assigned to ordered quality grades while keeping their meanings and order fixed. Each version retains links to its original instance, semantic-answer mapping, and intervention condition. Appendix D specifies the construction rules; Appendix A illustrates each type with paired task examples. Material Verification and Selection. Programmatic checks confirm candidate identities, grade mappings, and the target named by each external judgment. Image–text descriptions are checked against the image and task; irrelevant-information sets are checked for answer cues, task-relevant evidence, and added requirements. Appendix D specifies the review criteria and how exclusions affect paired instances. The final pool contains 5,323 original instances and 76,439 intervened instances, for 81,762 model inputs. Appendix E breaks these counts down by source, task, interface, and intervention condition. 3.4 Evaluation Metrics We measure intervention effects at the dataset and instance levels. Dataset-level task performance uses accuracy (Acc) for choice and yes/no judgment, and Spearman rank correlation coefficient ( ρ \rho ) for scoring; accuracy change ( Δ ​ Acc \Delta\mathrm{Acc} ) measures the net performance shift. Instance-level metrics characterize changes to individual decisions: semantic flip rate (FR) measures decision stability, while error introduction rate (EIR) and error correction rate (ECR) distinguish effects on originally correct and incorrect instances. Semantic Flip Rate (FR). FR measures the proportion of paired instances whose semantic decision changes under an intervention. Let 𝒫 b , v \mathcal{P}_{b,v} be the set of original–intervened pairs with valid predictions in both conditions, and let i i index the original instances in this set. Their semantic decisions are y ^ i ( 0 ) \hat{y}_{i}^{(0)} and y ^ i ( b , v ) \hat{y}_{i}^{(b,v)} . We define FR as FR b , v = 1 | 𝒫 b , v | ∑ i ∈ 𝒫 b , v [ y ^ i ( b , v ) ≠ y ^ i ( 0 ) ] , \mathrm{FR}_{b,v}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{b,v}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{b,v}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{i}^{(b,v)}\neq\hat{y}_{i}^{(0)}\right], (3) where 𝟏 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathbf{1}[\cdot] equals 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise. FR applies to all three decision interfaces. Lower FR indicates greater stability; unlike Δ ​ Acc \Delta\mathrm{Acc} , it captures paired decision changes even when aggregate accuracy remains unchanged. Accuracy change can conceal opposite effects on originally correct and incorrect instances. EIR and ECR separate these outcomes for external-judgment and image–text description interventions in choice and yes/no judgment tasks. Let 𝒫 b , v \mathcal{P}_{b,v} denote the set of original–intervened pairs with valid predictions in both conditions, and let y i ∗ y_{i}^{*} be the reference answer for instance i i . Error Introduction Rate (EIR). EIR measures the proportion of originally correct decisions that become incorrect under an incorrect external judgment or conflicting description: EIR b , v = ∑ i ∈ 𝒫 b , v [ y ^ i ( 0 ) = y i ∗ , y ^ i ( b , v ) ≠ y i ∗ ] ∑ i ∈ 𝒫 b , v [ y ^ i ( 0 ) = y i ∗ ] . \mathrm{EIR}_{b,v}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{b,v}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{i}^{(0)}=y_{i}^{*},\,\hat{y}_{i}^{(b,v)}\neq y_{i}^{*}\right]}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{b,v}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{i}^{(0)}=y_{i}^{*}\right]}. (4) Lower EIR indicates less harm from incorrect information. Error Correction Rate (ECR). ECR measures the proportion of originally incorrect decisions that become correct under a correct external judgment or consistent description: ECR b , v = ∑ i ∈ 𝒫 b , v [ y ^ i ( 0 ) ≠ y i ∗ , y ^ i ( b , v ) = y i ∗ ] ∑ i ∈ 𝒫 b , v [ y ^ i ( 0 ) ≠ y i ∗ ] . \mathrm{ECR}_{b,v}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{b,v}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{i}^{(0)}\neq y_{i}^{*},\,\hat{y}_{i}^{(b,v)}=y_{i}^{*}\right]}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{b,v}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{i}^{(0)}\neq y_{i}^{*}\right]}. (5) Higher ECR indicates greater benefit from correct information. Grade shifts and changes in probability assigned to an answer further characterize intervention effects; their computation is given in Appendix G .
