items.content: Information retrieval The science surrounding search engines is commonly referred to as information retrieval, in which algorithmic principles are developed to match user interests to the best information about those interests. Google started as a result of our founders' attempt to find the best matching between the user queries and Web documents, and do it really fast. During the process, they uncovered a few basic principles: 1) best pages tend to be those linked to the most; 2) best description of a page is often derived from the anchor text associated with the links to a page. Theories were developed to exploit these principles to optimize the task of retrieving the best documents for a user query. Search and Information Retrieval on the Web has advanced significantly from those early days: 1) the notion of ""information"" has greatly expanded from documents to much richer representations such as images, videos, etc., 2) users are increasingly searching on their Mobile devices with very different interaction characteristics from search on the Desktops; 3) users are increasingly looking for direct information, such as answers to a question, or seeking to complete tasks, such as appointment booking. Through our research, we are continuing to enhance and refine the world's foremost search engine by aiming to scientifically understand the implications of those changes and address new challenges that they bring. Recent Publications See More The Live Database: Firestore’s Scalable and Consistent Realtime Queries David Gay Ram Kesavan Namita Lal Per Jacobsson Hui Wu Matt Bell Xijiao Li 2026 Preview Preview abstract Google’s Firestore is a NoSQL serverless database service that scales to millions of queries per second and petabytes of storage, serving over 8 million databases and 1.5 billion monthly active end users. A key reason for its popularity is its unique realtime query feature, which greatly simplifes web and mobile application development. Realtime queries allow an application to present an up-to-date and strongly-consistent view of the state of the database to the end-user, and to receive fast notifications of changes to the database state. In this paper we present the architecture of the Firestore realtime stack, how it provides seamless scaling and high availability while supplying strongly-consistent responses to clients, including evaluations simulating workloads that represent large applications. We also explain how the Firestore SDK enables the application to deliver a smooth user experience through periods of network disconnection. View details Manifest-Assisted Retrieval in Artificial Intelligence Search: Evidence Gaps and a Security Evaluation Framework for llms.txt Iris Qian Varus Jing Rong "Ariel" Bao Annabel Yi Mark Zhou 2026 Preview Preview abstract No study identified in our audit measured the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary web or sitemap retrieval remained fixed. We audited 39 research papers, standards, specifications, product documents, and operational studies available through August 5, 2026. Direct evidence stops at publication and Hypertext Transfer Protocol request behavior: a purposive 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint, while a non-probability log study found that 97% of valid-file domains received no requests in May 2026. We separate publication, fetch, model use, and action; define five operational threat paths and paired security–utility estimands; and exercise deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. The resulting framework measures a manifest-specific effect View details QBAT: Model-based Query Budget Autotuner for Clustering-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Jonghyun Bae Tae Jun Ham Alan Li Supawit Chockchowwat Yannis Papakonstantinou Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment (2026), pp. 3091-3104 Preview Preview abstract Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is a critical component in modern data-intensive applications, but its performance is often hindered by the use of a static query budget parameter. This one-size-fits-all approach, even if well-tuned, fails to account for the varying difficulty of individual queries, inevitably leading to suboptimal latency on easy queries and poor accuracy on hard ones. This paper introduces QBAT, a query-aware budget autotuner designed to resolve this dilemma. By analyzing query-specific features offline, QBAT dynamically allocates an appropriate budget for each query. We explore two predictive models: a highly accurate gradient-boosted decision tree and a simple, interpretable heuristic formula derived using the AlphaEvolve framework. These models can optimize budget allocation for both system performance or recall consistency priorities. Evaluations on large-scale datasets demonstrate that QBAT reduces total searched budget by up to 68.8% in the consistency mode on ScaNN, the state-of-the-art clustering-based ANNS method, while simultaneously enforcing a strict per-query recall target, a scenario where static budgets are notoriously inefficient and wasteful. View details UniGeoCLIP: Unified Geospatial Contrastive Learning Guillaume Astruc Eduard Trulls Jan Hosang Loic Landrieu Paul-Edouard Sarlin EarthVision Workshop at CVPR (2026) Preview Preview abstract The growing availability of co-located geospatial data spanning aerial imagery, street-level views, elevation models, text, and geographic coordinates offers a unique opportunity for multimodal representation learning. We introduce UNIGEOCLIP, a massively multimodal contrastive framework to jointly align five complementary geospatial modalities in a single unified embedding space. Unlike prior approaches that fuse modalities or rely on a central pivot representation, our method performs all-to-all contrastive alignment, enabling seamless comparison, retrieval, and reasoning across arbitrary combinations of modalities. We further propose a scaled latitude-longitude encoder that improves spatial representation by capturing multi-scale geographic structure. Extensive experiments across downstream geospatial tasks demonstrate that UNIGEOCLIP consistently outperforms single-modality contrastive models and coordinate-only baselines, highlighting the benefits of holistic multimodal geospatial alignment. A reference implementation is available at https://gastruc.github.io/unigeoclip. View details Breaking the Loop: An Empirical Comparison of Strategies for Novelty and Freshness in YouTube Music Robin Dumas Gergo Varady Murat Goksedef Srivaths Ranganathan Tracy Pesin Zihuan Diao Josh Moore Yanwei Song Mukai Lu Bernardo Cunha 2026 Preview Preview abstract Continuously trained ranking models in music recommenders fall into feedback loops where previously consumed items dominate recommendations. This suppresses two distinct content classes: new releases (temporal freshness) and unlistened catalog items (novelty). Industry practitioners have a wide menu of interventions available, ranging from serving-time heuristics, training-data reweighting, architectural debiasing, to uncertainty-driven exploration, Each of which are well understood in academic settings. But live systems offer challenges with continuously ingested content, interconnected components, and practical limitations that counteract the findings from academic research. We report online A/B results for six interventions and one combination experiment across four conceptual layers (serving, training, architecture, exploration) on the YouTube Music homepage. All interventions modify the ranking model or the serving layer that consumes it scores; candidate generation and other upstream components are held fixed. Architectural debiasing produced the largest reduction in popularity dominance but penalized new releases. Uncertainty-driven exploration with an SNGP head drove +7.7\% Day-1 new-release engagement at no measurable homepage cost, at the expense of artist diversity. This study measures that inclusion event. SearchInject scores each candidate using ranker relevance, query-aligned search-abuse cues, instruction likelihood, and two relevance interactions. A threshold selected under a 0.5% clean-candidate false-positive ceiling determines which candidates are withheld before context assembly. The evaluation covers four spam-inspired page constructions, 300 untouched SciFact queries, and three retrievers, giving 1,200 transformation–query cases per retriever. The automated endpoint confirms no task hijacks and leaves 48 case-level judgments unresolved, so the trace cannot support an attack-success comparison. For the four evaluated constructions, the search-side rule removes most crafted pages with little measured loss in clean ranking. items.raw_text: Information retrieval The science surrounding search engines is commonly referred to as information retrieval, in which algorithmic principles are developed to match user interests to the best information about those interests. Google started as a result of our founders' attempt to find the best matching between the user queries and Web documents, and do it really fast. During the process, they uncovered a few basic principles: 1) best pages tend to be those linked to the most; 2) best description of a page is often derived from the anchor text associated with the links to a page. Theories were developed to exploit these principles to optimize the task of retrieving the best documents for a user query. Search and Information Retrieval on the Web has advanced significantly from those early days: 1) the notion of ""information"" has greatly expanded from documents to much richer representations such as images, videos, etc., 2) users are increasingly searching on their Mobile devices with very different interaction characteristics from search on the Desktops; 3) users are increasingly looking for direct information, such as answers to a question, or seeking to complete tasks, such as appointment booking. Through our research, we are continuing to enhance and refine the world's foremost search engine by aiming to scientifically understand the implications of those changes and address new challenges that they bring. Recent Publications See More The Live Database: Firestore’s Scalable and Consistent Realtime Queries David Gay Ram Kesavan Namita Lal Per Jacobsson Hui Wu Matt Bell Xijiao Li 2026 Preview Preview abstract Google’s Firestore is a NoSQL serverless database service that scales to millions of queries per second and petabytes of storage, serving over 8 million databases and 1.5 billion monthly active end users. A key reason for its popularity is its unique realtime query feature, which greatly simplifes web and mobile application development. Realtime queries allow an application to present an up-to-date and strongly-consistent view of the state of the database to the end-user, and to receive fast notifications of changes to the database state. In this paper we present the architecture of the Firestore realtime stack, how it provides seamless scaling and high availability while supplying strongly-consistent responses to clients, including evaluations simulating workloads that represent large applications. We also explain how the Firestore SDK enables the application to deliver a smooth user experience through periods of network disconnection. View details Manifest-Assisted Retrieval in Artificial Intelligence Search: Evidence Gaps and a Security Evaluation Framework for llms.txt Iris Qian Varus Jing Rong "Ariel" Bao Annabel Yi Mark Zhou 2026 Preview Preview abstract No study identified in our audit measured the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary web or sitemap retrieval remained fixed. We audited 39 research papers, standards, specifications, product documents, and operational studies available through August 5, 2026. Direct evidence stops at publication and Hypertext Transfer Protocol request behavior: a purposive 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint, while a non-probability log study found that 97% of valid-file domains received no requests in May 2026. We separate publication, fetch, model use, and action; define five operational threat paths and paired security–utility estimands; and exercise deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. The resulting framework measures a manifest-specific effect View details QBAT: Model-based Query Budget Autotuner for Clustering-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Jonghyun Bae Tae Jun Ham Alan Li Supawit Chockchowwat Yannis Papakonstantinou Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment (2026), pp. 3091-3104 Preview Preview abstract Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is a critical component in modern data-intensive applications, but its performance is often hindered by the use of a static query budget parameter. This one-size-fits-all approach, even if well-tuned, fails to account for the varying difficulty of individual queries, inevitably leading to suboptimal latency on easy queries and poor accuracy on hard ones. This paper introduces QBAT, a query-aware budget autotuner designed to resolve this dilemma. By analyzing query-specific features offline, QBAT dynamically allocates an appropriate budget for each query. We explore two predictive models: a highly accurate gradient-boosted decision tree and a simple, interpretable heuristic formula derived using the AlphaEvolve framework. These models can optimize budget allocation for both system performance or recall consistency priorities. Evaluations on large-scale datasets demonstrate that QBAT reduces total searched budget by up to 68.8% in the consistency mode on ScaNN, the state-of-the-art clustering-based ANNS method, while simultaneously enforcing a strict per-query recall target, a scenario where static budgets are notoriously inefficient and wasteful. View details UniGeoCLIP: Unified Geospatial Contrastive Learning Guillaume Astruc Eduard Trulls Jan Hosang Loic Landrieu Paul-Edouard Sarlin EarthVision Workshop at CVPR (2026) Preview Preview abstract The growing availability of co-located geospatial data spanning aerial imagery, street-level views, elevation models, text, and geographic coordinates offers a unique opportunity for multimodal representation learning. We introduce UNIGEOCLIP, a massively multimodal contrastive framework to jointly align five complementary geospatial modalities in a single unified embedding space. Unlike prior approaches that fuse modalities or rely on a central pivot representation, our method performs all-to-all contrastive alignment, enabling seamless comparison, retrieval, and reasoning across arbitrary combinations of modalities. We further propose a scaled latitude-longitude encoder that improves spatial representation by capturing multi-scale geographic structure. Extensive experiments across downstream geospatial tasks demonstrate that UNIGEOCLIP consistently outperforms single-modality contrastive models and coordinate-only baselines, highlighting the benefits of holistic multimodal geospatial alignment. A reference implementation is available at https://gastruc.github.io/unigeoclip. items.content: On 19 November 2026, the European Board for Digital Services (the Board) convened in Brussels for its 21st regular meeting. It held an in-depth discussion on online scams, adopted its Annual Work Programme for the year ahead and discussed, amongst other things the work on the updated Elections Guidelines and on the development of a crisis and incident protocol. During the meeting, the Board held a second in-depth discussion on online scams, reaffirming the importance of tackling this growing and serious risk for users of online platforms. Emphasizing the role of fraudulent advertising in the context of dissemination of scams, the Board welcomed the commitment by the European Commission to drafting guidelines in regard to Article 39 (3) DSA, with a view to streamline the structure of ad libraries and to enhance transparency for regulators and to facilitate independent third party review. In particular, the Board discussed the Commission’s engagement with relevant stakeholders from the financial sector, online platforms and other actors, to explore a possible Code of Conduct on online scams and fraud under Article 45 Digital Services Act (DSA), and in line with the forthcoming Payment Services Regulation. Furthermore, the Board has adopted its Annual Work Plan for 2027, setting out six priorities - three thematic and three horizontal ones - to guide its work in the year ahead. The Board reaffirms its commitment to a safe, predictable and trusted online environment that facilitates innovation and protects fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and the right to information. The work plan places the protection of EU citizens’ rights, particularly those of minors and consumers online, at the centre of its action. The thematic priorities focus on protecting minors online, strengthening consumer protection and tackling illegal content, and enhancing trust in the information space. Finally, the Board took note on the work on the revision of the DSA Election Guidelines , expected to be adopted before the end of the year. The Board also discussed the development of a DSA incidents protocol. Until the next meeting, the work of the Board will continue at technical level in the context of its different Working Groups . Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 19, 2026 Back to Top
